R1062.title: Unsafe return of Afghan nationals from Pakistan causes food, shelter and livelihood shortage upon their arrival at Afghanistan along with risk of persecution.
R1062.what_happened: In late May 2025, the forced repatriation of Afghan nationals from Pakistan intensified, triggering a growing humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan. Since Pakistan’s crackdown on undocumented foreigners in September 2023, over 850,000 Afghans have been...

evolution.impact_materialisation:
In late May 2025, the forced repatriation of Afghan nationals from Pakistan intensified, triggering a growing humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan. Since Pakistan’s crackdown on undocumented foreigners in September 2023, over 850,000 Afghans have been deported or have returned under pressure, with daily arrivals now averaging between 7,000–10,000 individuals. In response to the mounting crisis, the Afghan authorities, in collaboration with international humanitarian organisations, have launched an Integrated Response Plan for Returnees. This initiative aims to address both immediate needs – such as shelter, food, and medical assistance – and long-term reintegration challenges, including livelihood support and legal documentation.
Despite this, the situation remains dire. Upon arrival, most returnees are received in temporary camps that are already overcrowded and underresourced. In many cases, several families are forced to share a single tent. Access to clean water, sanitation, and healthcare is severely limited, heightening health risks, particularly among children and older people.
Women and girls face some of the harshest consequences of the return. An estimated 150,000 school-age girls have returned since the crackdown began, most of whom remain barred from attending school owing to Taliban-imposed restrictions. Women-headed households, in particular, face heightened economic insecurity, as women are banned from working in most sectors, severely limiting their ability to provide for their families.
Children are also critically affected. Reports indicate that over 250,000 children returning from Pakistan are in urgent need of shelter, food, and education. Approximately 65% of them are currently not enrolled in school, primarily given a lack of documentation or gender-based restrictions. Alarmingly, 99% of returnee families report insufficient food to last more than a few weeks.
Human rights defenders, former government workers, and those with ties to foreign military forces face serious protection risks, including arbitrary detention and persecution. There are also widespread reports of abuse, including extortion by Pakistani authorities during detention and deportation processes.
Projections suggest that if Pakistan’s deportation campaign continues unchecked, tens of thousands more will be forced to return, potentially overwhelming Afghanistan’s already fragile infrastructure and deepening its humanitarian crisis.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 08/05/2025
Between April and early May 2025, the forced return of Afghan nationals from Pakistan intensified, aggravating humanitarian challenges in Afghanistan. In April alone, over 118,400 Afghans returned, including approximately 25,600 deportees. The majority of these returnees are undocumented individuals, constituting 72% of the April returns, followed by Afghan Citizen Card holders (22%) and Proof of Registration cardholders (6%). Women and girls constitute approximately 49% of the returnees. Many arrive with limited resources, facing immediate shortages in food, shelter, and livelihoods. A significant number report difficulties in securing basic necessities, with many unable to return to their original provinces or districts, compounding their vulnerability. The situation is particularly dire for women, children, and minority groups, who face heightened risks of persecution and exploitation upon return, particularly given the current sociopolitical situation in Afghanistan.
Despite many organisations providing support with basic urgent needs, the huge number of returnees are anticipated to face severe shortages of food, housing, and healthcare, along with protection risks, in the coming days. Considering the urgent needs of returnees, organisations such as IOM, UNHCR, and IFRC have launched emergency appeals, highlighting the need for further protection and integration concerns.

R1062.title: The escalation of political and armed conflict in Southwest state leads to large‑scale displacement and worsens humanitarian conditions
R1062.what_happened: The clashes and prolonged fear of wider confrontation triggered pre-emptive mass displacement of over 50,000 people, predominantly women and children, from Baidoa towards Burhakaba, Hudur, Waajid, and surrounding areas. Three people were killed and f...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: On 30 March 2026, federal forces backed by allied clan militias entered Baidoa following weeks of escalating political tensions, engaging in brief but heavy clashes with Southwest State regional forces before assuming control of the city. Southwest State President Laftagareen resigned and fled to Kenya. Further clashes between federal forces and Laftagareen loyalists erupted on the outskirts of Baidoa in late May 2026. Elections in Southwest State are currently underway amid continued instability. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))
evolution.impact_materialisation: The clashes and prolonged fear of wider confrontation triggered pre-emptive mass displacement of over 50,000 people, predominantly women and children, from Baidoa towards Burhakaba, Hudur, Waajid, and surrounding areas. Three people were killed and five injured. Schools, hospitals, and maternal and child health centres were temporarily closed. Displaced populations faced heightened protection risks including overcrowding, inadequate shelter, and gender-based violence exposure, compounding already severe drought-related displacement and food insecurity across Bay and Bakool. Some families have begun returning, though conditions remain fragile. Broader risks related to the federal–state constitutional tensions are captured under the Somalia constitutional crisis risk. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))

R1062.title: Failure of essential services owing to the blockade in Mali leads to civil unrest and destabilisation and aggravates needs
R1062.what_happened: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several region...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: JNIM's blockade strategy expanded beyond northern and central Mali into southern and western regions, targeting fuel convoys, transport corridors, and economic infrastructure. The blockade persisted throughout the monitoring period despite temporary fluctuations in fuel availability and continued to disrupt national supply chains and state control over key transport routes.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several regions. While large-scale civil unrest did not materialise, the blockade contributed to worsening humanitarian conditions, weakened state authority, and increased insecurity. Ongoing blockade-related dynamics are now captured under the new Mali risk on coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 27/04/2026
The risk remains high and increasingly volatile. While there were indications of a partial easing in the intensity of the fuel blockade earlier in April 2026, recent large-scale coordinated attacks across multiple cities highlight a renewed deterioration in the security environment. Attacks targeting key locations, including Kati near Bamako, and the reported death of the Minister of Defence underscore the extent of armed groups’ operational reach. These developments are likely to further undermine the State’s ability to secure key transport corridors and ensure the continuity of fuel supply, which remains heavily dependent on military-escorted convoys. The reported loss of control over areas such as Kidal and the withdrawal of allied forces also point to weakening state authority in strategic regions. As a result, the risk of renewed disruptions to fuel supply and essential services remains high. Combined with continued fuel price increases and inflationary pressures, this may further constrain access to electricity, healthcare, and markets, while increasing the likelihood of social tensions. Overall, recent events suggest that earlier improvements were fragile and that the structural drivers of the risk remain firmly in place. ([RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [RFI 02/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260402-mali-autorit%C3%A9s-accusent-des-entreprises-utiliser-crise-carburant-pour-gonfler-leurs-prix), [BBC 24/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/afrique/articles/cyv1rpn4753o), [Ledjely 01/04/2026](https://ledjely.com/2026/04/01/mali-la-hausse-du-carburant-fait-craindre-une-spirale-des-prix/), [Timbuktu Institute 17/04/2026](https://timbuktu-institute.org/index.php/toutes-l-actualites/item/1509-le-mali-entre-chocs-externes-et-defis-internes))


UPDATE 30/03/2026
The risk has slightly deteriorated, with more fuel shortages reported. On 28 March 2026, the Government of Mali raised diesel prices by nearly 30% and petrol prices by 13% in response to supply disruptions by the Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin blockade. The heightened impacts of the fuel shortages increase the likelihood of civil unrest. On 25 March, diesel shortages in Bamako intensified as limited fuel imports were further redirected to support electricity generation during a heat wave. Several fuel stations ran out of diesel, leading to long queues at remaining supply points and disrupting urban mobility. At least 100 public transport vehicles were taken out of service, while construction-related transport (e.g. sand and gravel trucks) halted. ([TRT 10/03/2026](https://www.trtafrika.com/article/27f0213a3997), [Bloomberg 28/03/2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-28/mali-raises-petrol-diesel-prices-and-cuts-some-fuel-subsidies))


UPDATE 26/02/2026
Since January, the risk linked to the fuel blockade and related insecurity has remained high and volatile, with continued attacks despite temporary supply improvements in Bamako. While fuel availability in the capital improved in early February, the broader trend points to sustained operational disruption and geographic expansion of insecurity.  Key developments include renewed large-scale JNIM attacks on fuel convoys near Kayes, leading to the killing of drivers and military escorts and prompting a nationwide transport strike on 9 February. In central Mali, state forces conducted airstrikes in Macina (Ségou Region) following reported insurgent activity in Sikasso, while in Kidal region, a convoy was targeted by both JNIM and Azawad Liberation Front elements, suggesting overlapping armed actor pressure in the north. Continued road blockades affecting multiple localities and persistent electricity shortages (6–8 hours per day in Bamako) indicate structural fragility. In the short to medium term, continued convoy insecurity and transport disruptions risk renewed fuel shortages, rising prices, reduced market access, and further constraints on electricity supply, livelihoods, and humanitarian access, particularly outside the capital. ([DW 10/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/fr/focus-sahel-plus-villes-sous-blocus-du-jnim-au-mali/a-75901357), [RFI 03/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260203-au-mali-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-plie-mais-ne-rompt-pas), [RFI 10/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260210-mali-cibles-d-attaques-jihadistes-des-chauffeurs-routiers-appellent-%C3%A0-un-arr%C3%AAt-de-travail), [RFI 20/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260220-mali-une-frappe-de-drone-des-rebelles-du-fla-contre-l-arm%C3%A9e-fait-des-morts-des-deux-c%C3%B4t%C3%A9s)). 


UPDATE 02/02/2026
Since the previous update, the risk associated with the fuel blockade has remained elevated but volatile, with short-lived improvements followed by renewed disruption. While some fuel circulation has resumed intermittently, shortages persisted throughout January 2026, indicating neither clear escalation nor stabilisation. Key developments point to a broadening of the blockade’s scope. In Bamako, electricity supply remains limited to around five to seven hours per day, and fuel availability continues to be intermittent, with long queues and growing reliance on informal markets. In the southwest, Nioro du Sahel remains under a near-total blockade since early September 2025, with movement restrictions, reported abductions, and the increasing scarcity of food, medicines, fuel, and water. In parallel, attacks linked to Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin have expanded beyond fuel convoys to economic infrastructure, including mid-January 2026 attacks on industrial sites in Kayes and late January attacks on fuel convoys. Authorities have announced tighter fuel controls and reinforced escorts ahead of Ramadan, but continued incidents suggest a persistent risk of disruption to essential services, rising living costs, constrained access to markets, and increasing humanitarian needs in affected urban and blockaded areas. ([RFI 10/01/2026)[https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260110-mali-des-habitants-de-nioro-du-sahel-racontent-le-blocus-jihadiste-qui-dure-depuis-cinq-mois), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-la-fourniture-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-de-carburant-reste-tr%C3%A8s-insuffisante-les-bamakois-se-r%C3%A9signent), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-le-manque-de-carburant-%C3%A0-l-a%C3%A9roport-de-bamako-perturbe-certaines-liaisons), [RFI 16/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260116-mali-blocus-jihadiste-%C3%A0-nioro-du-sahel-la-situation-est-sous-contr%C3%B4le-selon-les-autorit%C3%A9s-de-transition), [RFI 12/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260112-mali-comment-et-pourquoi-des-jihadistes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-trois-sites-industriels-de-la-r%C3%A9gion-de-kayes), [RFI 02/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260202-au-mali-les-autorit%C3%A9s-veulent-s%C3%A9curiser-l-apprivisionnement-de-carburant-pour-le-mois-de-ramadan))


UPDATE 18/12/2025
Since early December, the JNIM has resumed attacks on fuel convoys after a temporary slowdown observed in late November. The initial lull allowed some fuel deliveries to reach Bamako and Mopti, briefly reducing shortages and restoring limited electricity and public services. However, renewed ambushes in Bougouni, Ouélessébougou, and Ségou, including the destruction of over 15 fuel tankers and the killing of drivers, have reinstated supply chain disruptions and public anxiety. In Bamako, queues at petrol stations have grown again, diesel has become scarce, and intermittent power cuts have returned. While 300 trucks were received ahead of the AES summit in mid-December, the improvement remains temporary. In Mopti and surrounding areas, fuel convoys have resumed under heavy military protection, but the quantities remain insufficient to meet the demand. Electricity has returned for around nine hours per day, and some economic activity has restarted, though fuel prices on the black market remain triple the official rate.  The blockade continues to affect humanitarian operations and access to essential services. In areas such as Koulikoro, Sikasso, and Koutiala, fuel scarcity persists, with limited electricity, inaccessible health services, and rising transport costs. The JNIM’s strategy has evolved beyond physical control, aiming to delegitimise the state through economic strangulation and selective violence. The group is reportedly consolidating control over rural areas by offering basic services (such as justice and security) under Islamic governance, gradually normalising its authority. 
([Echoes of the Sahel 17/12/2025](https://mailchi.mp/9406facccf81/sahel-news-round-up-21010886?e=fe2a2db667), [RFI 17/12/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251217-mali-%C3%A0-bamako-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-est-fluctuant), [RFI 12/12/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251212-mali-retour-du-carburant-et-du-courant-%C3%A0-mopti-une-am%C3%A9lioration-notable-mais-encore-trop-r%C3%A9duite), [Revue Conflicts 26/11/2025](https://www.revueconflits.com/jnim-au-mali-letranglement-de-bamako-et-la-strategie-du-califat-par-consentement/))

R1067.title: Resource-related clashes and political tensions in Tindouf camps restrict humanitarian access and increase protection risks for Sahrawi refugees
R1067.what_happened: The risk's hazard materialised, but the anticipated impact did not. The hazard was evident in August, with an armed clash within the Polisario Front on 7 August and two peaceful protests on 15 August over detainee treatment and perceived unequal acce...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The risk's hazard materialised, but the anticipated impact did not. The hazard was evident in August, with an armed clash within the Polisario Front on 7 August and two peaceful protests on 15 August over detainee treatment and perceived unequal access to medical evacuation. These developments were consistent with the risk's anticipated resource-related and political tensions. In September, pressure remained evident, including allegations of mismanagement in medical evacuations, while political pressure around the Tindouf camps continued, including Morocco's 9 September call for durable solutions and Spain's 10 September approval of a nationality bill potentially affecting Sahrawis. Despite this, the anticipated humanitarian impact – major disruption to aid distribution, water, health services, or camp administration – did not materialise. ACLED recorded no fatalities from the August incidents, and the monitoring does not indicate significant disruption to humanitarian operations or large-scale displacement. ([ACLED accessed 04/10/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [Al3omk 02/09/2026](https://al3omk.com/1183989.html), [Attassia 02/09/2026](https://attasiaa.com/%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%85%d8%ba%d8%b1%d8%a8-%d9%8a%d9%82%d8%aa%d8%b1%d8%ad-%d8%ab%d9%84%d8%a7%d8%ab%d8%a9-%d8%ad%d9%84%d9%88%d9%84-%d9%84%d9%85%d8%ae%d9%8a%d9%85%d8%a7%d8%aa-%d8%aa%d9%86%d8%af%d9%88%d9%81/), [AJ 13/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/13/why-spains-new-sahrawi-citizenship-law-matters-to-morocco), [MCD 25/09/2026](https://www.mc-doualiya.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AE%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B1%D8%A9/20260925-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%AF%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B0%D9%91%D8%B1-%D9%85%D9%86-%D8%AA%D8%AF%D9%87%D9%88%D8%B1-%D8%A3%D9%88%D8%B6%D8%A7%D8%B9-%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B2%D8%AD%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B5%D8%AD%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9-1))
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 07/09/2026
Political tensions within the Polisario Front intensified in August 2026. Ahead of the front's 17th General Congress, leader Ibrahim Ghali delivered increasingly hardline rhetoric at the youth and student conferences between 6–7 August, framing international pressure around UNSC Resolution 2797 as a ‘conspiracy’ and calling supporters to ‘close ranks’. This signals leadership actively managing internal dissent rather than consolidating authority, affirming leadership fragmentation. Separately, two sit-ins were held at the Tindouf camps from 16–17 August over social and humanitarian complaints directed at Polisario leadership, confirming that camp-level frustration is translating into organised protest. ([AJ 07/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/amp/news/2026/8/7), [Hespress 17/08/2026](https://www.hespress.com/%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%85%D8%AA%D8%B2%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%86%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B2-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%B6%D8%B9-%D9%82%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%AF%D8%A9-1793456.html))


UPDATE 02/08/2026
The risk has deteriorated. Since late July 2026, fires have destroyed vehicles of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Saguia el Hamra and Rio de Oro (Polisario) in both Smara and the Rabouni administrative headquarters, with local accounts alleging retaliatory acts linked to tribal tensions and disputes over leadership positions ahead of the 17th Polisario Congress – suggesting intra-camp tensions are moving from interpersonal disputes towards organised confrontations affecting governance infrastructure. This coincides with a WFP-confirmed funding shortage expected to halt food distributions by September, threatening food assistance for over 80% of the 133,672 Sahrawi refugees dependent on humanitarian aid across Algeria, likely to intensify competition over diminishing resources within camps. Internationally, mounting pressure around Polisario's legal status, including a US House bill gaining co-sponsors and 11 members of the European Parliament calling for a terrorist-designation assessment, and Spain's postponement of the Sahrawi citizenship bill add political uncertainty at a moment when camp governance is already under strain, increasing the likelihood of further instability ahead of the congress in late 2026. ([Yabiladi 22/07/2026](https://ar.yabiladi.com/articles/details/199090/%D8%AD%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%82-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D8%AA%D8%B7%D8%A7%D9%84-%D9%85%D9%82%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%88.html), [WFP 21/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/algeria/wfp-algeria-country-brief-july-2026-reporting-period-june-2026), [24saa 13/07/2026](https://24saa.com/%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B6%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%85-%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%AC%D8%AF%D9%8A%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D9%88%D9%86%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%B3-%D9%8A%D8%B9%D8%B2%D8%B2/), [Alittihad 19/07/2026](https://alittihad.info/%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%84%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%A3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%86-%D9%8A%D8%AF%D8%B9%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%B1%D8%A8%D8%B7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3/), [Assahifa 13/07/2026](https://www.assahifa.com/%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D9%83%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%A9-%D9%84%D9%80%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D9%88%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%85-%D9%84%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%88/)).

This initiative aims to address both immediate needs – such as shelter, food, and medical assistance – and long-term reintegration challenges, including livelihood support and legal documentation.
Despite this, the situation remains dire. Upon arrival, most returnees are received in temporary camps that are already overcrowded and underresourced. In many cases, several families are forced to share a single tent. Access to clean water, sanitation, and healthcare is severely limited, heightening health risks, particularly among children and older people.
Women and girls face some of the harshest consequences of the return. An estimated 150,000 school-age girls have returned since the crackdown began, most of whom remain barred from attending school owing to Taliban-imposed restrictions. Women-headed households, in particular, face heightened economic insecurity, as women are banned from working in most sectors, severely limiting their ability to provide for their families.
Children are also critically affected. Reports indicate that over 250,000 children returning from Pakistan are in urgent need of shelter, food, and education. Approximately 65% of them are currently not enrolled in school, primarily given a lack of documentation or gender-based restrictions. Alarmingly, 99% of returnee families report insufficient food to last more than a few weeks.
Human rights defenders, former government workers, and those with ties to foreign military forces face serious protection risks, including arbitrary detention and persecution. There are also widespread reports of abuse, including extortion by Pakistani authorities during detention and deportation processes.
Projections suggest that if Pakistan’s deportation campaign continues unchecked, tens of thousands more will be forced to return, potentially overwhelming Afghanistan’s already fragile infrastructure and deepening its humanitarian crisis.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 08/05/2025
Between April and early May 2025, the forced return of Afghan nationals from Pakistan intensified, aggravating humanitarian challenges in Afghanistan. In April alone, over 118,400 Afghans returned, including approximately 25,600 deportees. The majority of these returnees are undocumented individuals, constituting 72% of the April returns, followed by Afghan Citizen Card holders (22%) and Proof of Registration cardholders (6%). Women and girls constitute approximately 49% of the returnees. Many arrive with limited resources, facing immediate shortages in food, shelter, and livelihoods. A significant number report difficulties in securing basic necessities, with many unable to return to their original provinces or districts, compounding their vulnerability. The situation is particularly dire for women, children, and minority groups, who face heightened risks of persecution and exploitation upon return, particularly given the current sociopolitical situation in Afghanistan.
Despite many organisations providing support with basic urgent needs, the huge number of returnees are anticipated to face severe shortages of food, housing, and healthcare, along with protection risks, in the coming days. Considering the urgent needs of returnees, organisations such as IOM, UNHCR, and IFRC have launched emergency appeals, highlighting the need for further protection and integration concerns.

R1043.title: Tensions between the military and political components in Sudan’s transitional government result in social unrest and increased access constraints for humanitarian organisations
R1043.what_happened: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed th...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed the pipeline that carries oil to Khartoum. The pipeline was reopened after two days, following a meeting with government officials. In response, Arab tribes in Kassala state protested against the Beja tribes’ blocking of roads and ports. The Beja tribes continued to block Red Sea ports and highways connecting eastern Sudan with the rest of the country until mid-October 2021. The Government warned that the country was running out of life-saving medicines, fuel, and wheat stocks.

R1043.title: The deployment of the regional military force leads to more displacement and increased humanitarian needs in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
R1043.what_happened: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian cri...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: In response to the escalating activities of armed groups, including the March 23 Movement (M23), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) dispatched the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF) in November 2022. This multinational force, comprising troops from Kenya, Burundi, South Sudan, and Uganda, was deployed to bring stability to the conflict-torn eastern regions of the DRC. However, the presence of the EACRF led to heightened clashes between military forces and various armed factions, exacerbating security challenges in the region. These clashes caused a large number of civilians to leave conflict zones, increasing the need for humanitarian aid in the region. The departure of the EACRF in December 2023 created a security gap that was swiftly taken advantage of by armed groups, further exacerbating instability.
evolution.impact_materialisation: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian crisis, with critical needs in areas such as shelter, food, water, sanitation, and medical care. The situation has been aggravated by the suspension of activities by numerous humanitarian organisations due to persistent insecurity.

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Since late 2022, there has been a significant increase in violent incidents attributed to non-state armed groups in the northern regions of West African coastal countries, particularly Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, and Togo. Between October 2022 and January 2023, more than 73 such incidents were reported, representing a sharp increase compared to around 30 incidents during the same period the previous year. These incidents include attacks on civilians and security forces, kidnappings, destruction of property, and the use of improvised explosive devices.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The increase in violence has caused internal displacement in the affected countries. In Benin, at least 1,200 internally displaced people (IDPs) have been reported in the Atacora Department. In Togo, over 2,200 IDPs have been recorded in the Savanes region. Despite the rise in insecurity, food insecurity levels remain relatively stable between October and December 2022 compared to the same period in 2021. However, the continued growth of armed groups represents a significant threat to food security. Ongoing violence disrupts agricultural activities and access to markets, potentially exacerbating food insecurity in the near future.

evolution.hazard_materialisation: On 30 March 2026, federal forces backed by allied clan militias entered Baidoa following weeks of escalating political tensions, engaging in brief but heavy clashes with Southwest State regional forces before assuming control of the city. Southwest State President Laftagareen resigned and fled to Kenya. Further clashes between federal forces and Laftagareen loyalists erupted on the outskirts of Baidoa in late May 2026. Elections in Southwest State are currently underway amid continued instability. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))
evolution.impact_materialisation: The clashes and prolonged fear of wider confrontation triggered pre-emptive mass displacement of over 50,000 people, predominantly women and children, from Baidoa towards Burhakaba, Hudur, Waajid, and surrounding areas. Three people were killed and five injured. Schools, hospitals, and maternal and child health centres were temporarily closed. Displaced populations faced heightened protection risks including overcrowding, inadequate shelter, and gender-based violence exposure, compounding already severe drought-related displacement and food insecurity across Bay and Bakool. Some families have begun returning, though conditions remain fragile. Broader risks related to the federal–state constitutional tensions are captured under the Somalia constitutional crisis risk. R1059.title: Intensified territorial disputes among armed groups over illegal mining corridors in southern Bolívar lead to mass displacement and confinement

evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 30/04/2026
The risk of escalation in southern Bolívar remains sustained, with the continued consolidation of non-state armed group control and the increasing use of explosive devices (such as improvised explosive devices [IEDs]) and drones intensifying protection risks. Armed groups have strengthened their presence across the Serranía de San Lucas, expanding territorial control through recruitment, threats, confinement, killings, and displacement. This reflects a broader loss of state control and the entrenchment of violence across critical mining areas.
The use of IEDs and drone-based attacks has become more prominent in 2026, marking a shift in conflict dynamics compared to 2025. These tactics have caused direct damage to civilian infrastructure, including homes, schools, and rural water systems, while triggering displacement and confinement. This indicates increasing operational capacity and a likely continuation of remote and indiscriminate attacks affecting civilian populations.
In April, two security incidents, including an armed confrontation and an attack, affected at least 133 people. At the same time, the onset of the rainy season is increasing the risk of flooding in already-vulnerable areas, particularly among communities historically exposed to inundations.
In the short term, the combined effects of armed violence and seasonal flooding are likely to increase humanitarian needs, restrict mobility, and further limit access to essential services and assistance. ([OCHA accessed 30/04/2026](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [El Original 29/04/2026](https://eloriginal.co/abril-lluvias-mil-garzas-anuncian-el-diluvio-bolivar-se-prepara-para-un-invierno-peligroso/), [OCHA 14/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/colombia/colombia-informe-de-situacion-humanitaria-2026-datos-acumulados-entre-enero-febrero-de-2026-fecha-de-publicacion-14-de-abril-de-2026), [FIP 22/04/2026](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/investigaciones-analisis/2026-04/las-alertas-detras-del-mapa-de-10-zonas-criticas-en-seguridad-y-control-estatal)) 


UPDATE 25/03/2026
The risk of escalation in southern Bolívar remains sustained, with increased use of explosive-laden drones intensifying conflict dynamics and protection risks. Clashes between the National Liberation Army (ELN), the Gaitanist Army of Colombia (EGC), and dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC-EP) continue as they compete for control of illegal mining corridors, triggering displacement and heightened insecurity in rural areas.
In March 2026, armed groups demonstrated growing operational capacity through the use of drones equipped with explosive devices, including an attack on a military helicopter that injured 12 soldiers. The dismantling of a training camp in Cantagallo revealed structured efforts to train combatants in drone-based attacks and explosive ordnance use, indicating increasing technological adaptation and a likely continuation of remote attacks. Simultaneously, the discovery of more than 15 bodies in Santa Rosa del Sur, linked to armed confrontations, highlights the intensity and lethality of current disputes over strategic corridors. These developments coincide with continued displacement in municipalities such as Arenal and persistent territorial contestation, particularly over river routes critical for mobility and supply chains. In the short term, the increased use of drones and explosive devices is likely to expand the geographical reach of violence, heighten risks to civilians and infrastructure, and further restrict movement and humanitarian access, particularly in rural communities.
([RCN 28/02/2026](https://www.noticiasrcn.com/colombia/ataque-a-helicoptero-del-ejercito-en-bolivar-deja-8-militares-heridos-996915), [La FM 01/03/2026](https://www.lafm.com.co/orden-publico/consejo-de-seguridad-en-bolivar-tras-atentado-a-helicoptero-de-ejercito-y-hechos-violentos-392040), [Corrillos 21/03/2026](https://www.corrillos.com.co/hallazgo-de-15-cuerpos-profundiza-violencia-en-santa-rosa-del-sur-bolivar/), [El Frente 20/03/2026](https://elfrente.com.co/terror-en-sur-de-bolivar-hallados-16-cadaveres-en-descomposicion/), [Seguimiento.co 20/03/2026](https://seguimiento.co/colombia/cae-centro-de-drones-y-explosivos-del-clan-del-golfo-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-85054))


UPDATE 27/02/2026
The risk of escalation in southern Bolívar remains sustained, with continued armed confrontations, new displacement, and compounding climatic shocks increasing humanitarian needs. In February 2026, mass displacement was reported in Arenal, with families from high lands fleeing to the urban centre following direct threats from non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and fear of being caught in clashes and bombardments. This represents recurrent displacement, as some of the affected population had already been displaced in 2025, indicating protracted vulnerability.
Social and human rights organisations issued an early warning on 12 February 2026 highlighting the intensification of clashes among NSAGs and the severe impact on agro-mining communities, including forced displacement, livelihood disruptions, and violations of international humanitarian law. The security situation has further deteriorated since the groups started using explosive-laden drones. On 6 February, the overflowing of the Caribona River and Santo Domingo Stream affected Montecristo and Arenal, creating a double-impact emergency. Floods, erosion, and climate variability affected over 15,000 people across Bolívar, while local capacities remain saturated.
In the short term, the overlap of conflict and flooding is likely to increase confinement, disrupt livelihoods, heighten protection risks for children, and further constrain humanitarian access. ([Caracol Radio 05/02/2026](https://caracol.com.co/2026/02/05/emergencia-humanitaria-en-arenal-desplazamientos-masivos-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-por-fuertes-combates/), [IFM Noticias 14/02/2026](https://ifmnoticias.com/organizaciones-de-derechos-humanos-denunciaron-escalada-de-violencia-en-el-sur-de-bolivar/), [Alerta Cartagena 04/02/2026](https://cartagena.alerta.com.co/judiciales/desplazamientos-en-arenal-al-sur-de-bolivar-233669), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Ui8hMAnWs4K-pyZti5reCrsd-q2d8SHW/view), [El Colombiano 18/02/2026](https://www.elcolombiano.com/colombia/bolivar-calamidad-publica-municipios-lluvias-inundaciones-MP33697597))


UPDATE 30/01/2026
The risk of a further escalation of violence in southern Bolívar has intensified since December 2025, driven by shifts in non-state armed group financing, expanding territorial disputes, and overstretched state response capacities. As armed groups increasingly turn to illegal gold mining, incentivised by record-high global gold prices amid geopolitical uncertainty, the strategic value of mining corridors in southern Bolívar has increased, heightening competition and the probability of violent confrontation. At the same time, changes in territorial control have led to a rise in direct clashes, with violence becoming more systemic rather than selective. Confinements and forced displacement (both mass and individual) continue to increase, disproportionately affecting rural and riverine communities, while threats increasingly materialise through mobility restrictions rather than isolated acts of intimidation.
In late January 2026, the governor of Bolívar requested urgent national-level intervention, warning that the escalation has exceeded local and departmental response capacities, signalling a shift from a localised security challenge to a crisis requiring coordinated national action. In the short to medium term, continued escalation is likely to drive further displacement, restrict humanitarian access, undermine agriculture- and mining-based livelihoods, as well as deepen protection risks. The risk posed by explosive ordnance remains high, with no new demining programmes identified until January 2026 further limiting safe movement and access to services. [Las Dos Orillas 29/01/2026](https://www.las2orillas.co/la-peligrosa-fiebre-del-oro-amenaza-con-ser-mas-violenta-que-las-guerras-del-narcotrafico/), [3iS/EHP Colombia 05/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/colombia-contexto-humanitario-y-conflicto-armado-magdalena-medio-2025?_gl=1*yeipiw*_gcl_au*MTM1ODQ3NDQyNC4xNzY5MTEyNTg4*_ga*MTgzMDA5Njk2NC4xNzY5MTEyNTc2*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3Njk3ODczMjEkbzckZzAkdDE3Njk3ODczMjEkajYwJGwwJGgw), [El Tiempo 17/01/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/colombia/otras-ciudades/yamil-pide-a-petro-reunion-urgente-por-escalada-armada-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-y-advierte-riesgo-humanitario-por-disputas-territoriales-armadas-ilegales-3524954), [Semana 15/01/2026](https://www.semana.com/nacion/cartagena/articulo/crisis-de-orden-publico-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-va-en-aumento-gobernador-arana-pide-reunion-urgente-con-el-presidente-petro/202616/))


UPDATE 29/12/2025
The humanitarian crisis in southern Bolívar has escalated as non-state armed groups (NSAGs) consolidate territorial control through intensified violent tactics against civilians. Across the Serranía de San Lucas, displacement, confinement, and mobility restrictions have become primary tools for population control, positioning the region as one of Colombia’s most affected areas in 2025. Between January--November, confinement affected 20,894 people, mass displacement affected 5,078, and mass displacement affected 4,616 (OCHA accessed 11/12/2025).  The widespread use of explosive ordnance (EO) – including anti-personnel mines and improvised explosive devices – and the increasing use of weaponised drones aggravate this precarious environment.
The resulting EO contamination of schools, water points, and agricultural land has disrupted essential services and undermined livelihoods, driving acute food insecurity. Beyond physical threats, NSAGs exert control by intimidating community leaders and weakening local governance. These pressures are expected to intensify ahead of the 2026 electoral cycle, heightening risks of political coercion. The region’s difficult geography and poor health and goverment facility infrastructure continue to restrict humanitarian access, delaying life-saving assistance in territories where the Ombudsman’s Office has already issued high-risk early warnings given the expansion of illicit economies. ([OCHA accessed 11/12/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [OCHA accessed 22/12/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [OCHA 24/10/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/informe-de-tendencias-e-impacto-humanitario-en-2025-datos-acumulados-entre-enero-septiembre-de-2025-fecha-de-publicacion-24-de-octubre-de-2025-enes), [DP 10/02/2025](https://www.defensoria.gov.co/-/defensor%C3%ADa-del-pueblo-alerta-sobre-crisis-humanitaria-en-el-sur-de-bol%C3%ADvar), [PARES 06/03/2025](https://www.pares.com.co/sur-de-bolivar-entre-coca-oro-y-guerra/), 
[El Universal 15/12/2025](https://www.eluniversal.com.co/regional/bolivar/2025/12/15/crisis-de-violencia-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-reiteran-alertas-ante-autoridades/)) 


UPDATE 27/11/2025
The risk trend has deteriorated over the past month as nonstate armed groups have expanded mobility restrictions, attacks against civilians, and territorial control in southern Bolívar. Armed strikes, blockades on food and fuel, and the use of explosive-bearing drones have deepened confinement and disrupted access to services. Around 34,900 people experienced forced displacement, confinement, or mobility restrictions from January–November 2025. Key developments include a 4 November massacre in San Pablo targeting mining workers, increased pressure and threats against civic authorities, and the coercive use of children and adolescents in support roles. Armed groups are also assuming quasi-state functions, arbitrating community disputes and consolidating subregional dependence. Sustained mine contamination in Montecristo and Arenal, attacks on schools, the prolonged suspension of classes affecting 1,370 students, and the kidnapping of a community leader indicate continued escalation. Short- to medium-term impacts include worsening food insecurity as a result of blockades, reduced mobility, contaminated water sources, heightened psychological distress, and major constraints on humanitarian access and safe political participation ahead of 2026. ([OCHA 08/08/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/haiti/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-8-august-2025), [Cambio 06/08/2025](https://cambiocolombia.com/conflicto-armado-en-colombia/articulo/2025/8/ejercito-sur-bolivar-eln-clan-golfo-confinamiento-conflicto-armado/), [Caracol Radio 07/11/2025](https://caracol.com.co/2025/11/07/tres-muertos-dejo-presunta-incursion-armada-del-eln-en-una-mina-de-oro-del-sur-de-bolivar/), [DP 22/09/2025](https://alertasstg.blob.core.windows.net/alertas/013-25.pdf), [EE 06/10/2025](https://www.elespectador.com/colombia-20/paz-y-memoria/guerra-en-sur-de-bolivar-desplazados-vuelven-a-la-zona-donde-hay-minas-antipersonal-y-combates-entre-eln-y-clan-del-golfo/), [OCHA accessed 10/11/2024](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [OCHA accessed 27/11/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia))

R1059.title: US military build-up in the Caribbean triggers internal destabilisation in Venezuela and heightens humanitarian needs
R1059.what_happened: The US military operation against Venezuela — designated Operation Absolute Resolve — was carried out on 3 January 2026 by elements of the Delta Force, US Air Force, and US Navy. The operation culminated in the capture of Nicolás Maduro and his wife...

evolution.hazard_materialisation:
The US military operation against Venezuela — designated Operation Absolute Resolve — was carried out on 3 January 2026 by elements of the Delta Force, US Air Force, and US Navy. The operation culminated in the capture of Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores at a safe house in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, where both were apprehended while asleep. Maduro and Flores were subsequently transferred to New York, where they are currently facing narco-trafficking charges.
Maduro's capture had been widely anticipated to create a power vacuum within Venezuela, with competing factions of the Chavista movement potentially vying for control through force. However, this scenario did not materialise. Vice President Delcy Rodríguez swiftly assumed leadership of the Chavista movement and, through political agreements that appear to have received US endorsement, successfully stabilised the situation — averting a political crisis that could have escalated into internal armed conflict.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 01/04/2026
Four months following the capture of Nicolás Maduro and the transfer of government to Delcy Rodríguez, the overall risk environment in Venezuela remains stable with tentative signs of short-term improvement. No immediate risk of internal power struggles within Rodríguez's political circle has been identified, and no significant Chavista figures appear to be actively opposing the agreements reached between Rodríguez and US President Donald Trump, allowing the Venezuelan government to continue functioning with relative normalcy.
Economic conditions in Venezuela in 2026 also appear to be gradually improving, continuing the upward trajectory in household incomes that began in 2025. Additionally, the US Government's engagement in a conflict with Iran has necessitated a reallocation of military focus away from Venezuela, reducing the likelihood of naval blockades or further armed operations in the country in the near term — a development that further contributes to the current period of relative stability.
([BBC 01/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/mundo/articles/c36r5l25429o); [HumVenezuela 31/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/2025-follow-report-complex-humanitarian-emergency-venezuela-january-2026?_gl=1*utepnc*_gcl_au*NDg0NTgzNTEuMTc3NjM2OTYxMg..*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzcxNzY4NTQkbzkzJGcxJHQxNzc3MTc2ODY1JGo0OSRsMCRoMA))



UPDATE 31/03/2026
Three months after Nicolás Maduro's capture and Delcy Rodríguez's elevation to Interim President of Venezuela, the overall risk trend has shown a slight improvement. No signs of power struggles within the Rodríguez government have emerged, and figures seen as misaligned with the Trump administration's agenda seem to have been gradually pushed out of influential positions. Most notably, Vladimir Padrino López — one of Maduro's closest allies and a key figure in maintaining territorial control and military loyalty to the Socialist Party — was removed as Defense Minister after 14 years in the role. This marks a significant shift away from a Maduro and Chávez loyalist leadership toward a more politically neutral and ideologically independent cabinet. So far, his removal has not caused visible fractures or internal conflict within the armed forces.
These developments have been accompanied by the US Government's decision to reopen its Embassy in Venezuela, which had been closed since 2019. Despite these small gains, sustained US political and military pressure on Venezuela continues, highlighting the fragility of the current situation. The relationship between the two governments could quickly deteriorate and become much more confrontational if the Trump administration perceives non-compliance from Rodríguez and her cabinet.



UPDATE 26/02/2026
Two months after the capture of Nicolás Maduro by US forces and the installation of former Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez as Interim President, the overall risk trend in Venezuela has moved towards stabilisation. There are no immediate indications of power struggles within the Government's senior political leadership, nor a significant increase in non-state armed group (NSAG) activity, although the risk of rapid deterioration persists. The new authorities have implemented the economic agreements with the US, including the dispatch of at least 80 million barrels of oil — Venezuela's primary export — and high-level engagement with US political and economic figures to establish platforms for foreign direct investment. Also, Delcy's administratation have pushed for laws that dicriminilized political opposition and the release of more than 400 previously detained opposition leaders, as well as the reversal of key policies implemented under the Maduro administration. 
That said, the United States continues to maintain some naval forces off the Venezuelan coast and sustained political pressure through consistent public messaging from the Trump administration on the conduct expected of Rodríguez and her administration. This highlights the fragility of current political arrangements and the possibility of military tension escalating rapidly as it did in early 2026, increasing risks of limited access to food and health services, as well as displacement spikes and reduced access to humanitarian services in high-risk conflict areas.

UPDATE 28/01/2026
Since the capture of Nicolás Maduro by US forces and the installation of former vice-president Delcy Rodríguez as interim president, the overall risk environment has stabilised. There are no immediate indications of power struggles within Venezuela’s senior political leadership or a significant increase in non-state armed group activity. The new authorities have reached economic agreements with the US, including oil sales – Venezuela’s main export – and planned investments by US companies, alongside political measures such as the release of political prisoners and a partial normalisation of diplomatic relations.
That said, the US continues to maintain a military presence off the Venezuelan coast, sustaining pressure despite the current period of relative calm. At the same time, the interim government has publicly stated that US military intervention must end, highlighting the fragility of the current arrangements and the risk that tensions could escalate again with little warning, increasing the risk of limited access to food, health, and protection services, as well as displacement spikes and reduced access to humanitarian services in conflict areas. ([CNN 21/01/2026](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2026/01/21/venezuela/delcy-rodriguez-venezuela-eeuu-petroleo-300-millones-dolares-efe), [InSight Crime 22/01/2026](https://insightcrime.org/news/will-guerrillas-lose-haven-post-maduro-venezuela/), [El Tiempo 25/01/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/mundo/venezuela/delcy-rodriguez-basta-de-las-ordenes-de-washington-sobre-politicos-en-venezuela-3527009), [CNN 22/01/2026](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2026/01/22/venezuela/trump-mira-petroleo-rodriguez-demandas-trax)) 



UPDATE 07/01/2026
Since early January 2026, the risk trend has deteriorated sharply, shifting from potential destabilisation to an acute crisis. The US military's capture of Nicolás Maduro on 3 January, followed by Delcy Rodríguez's installation as interim president, has triggered immediate power struggles among Rodríguez, military leaders, and Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, who controls the police and colectivo networks.
Rodríguez has invited Washington to cooperate, stating that post-Maduro, Venezuela seeks an "agenda of cooperation" with the US Government, including in the energy sector. On 7 January, the US Department of Energy eased sanctions to permit Venezuelan oil transport to the US, indicating negotiation advances. That said, Cabello's defiant rhetoric, despite US President Donald Trump's threats, signals ideological pushback and risks colectivo mobilisation into militia violence and instability.
Cúcuta border crossings in Colombia hold steady at around 60,000 daily pendular movements, unchanged since 3 January, with official data and reports showing no displacement surge amid the turmoil. The risk outlook stays precarious, balancing between consolidation and fracture, depending on compliance in oil negotiations and sustained military cohesion. Pragmatic signals (such as Rodríguez's oil overtures and US sanctions relief) clash with military fragility, yielding a bifurcated short-term risk path. Oil deal progress and stabilised regime revenue for military salaries could keep needs high but without a sudden surge. That said, Cabello's opposition to Rodríguez's approach, plus delayed pay from stalled oil income, might ignite colectivo mobilisation, military splits, and conflict, leading to displacement spikes and restricted humanitarian access in conflict zones.
([Defense One 05/01/2026](https://www.defenseone.com/threats/2026/01/the-d-brief-january-05-2026/410450/#:~:text=), [CBS accessed 07/05/2025](https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/venezuela-maduro-capture-president-trump-senate-oil/), [Latina Republic 05/01/2026](https://latinarepublic.com/2026/01/05/colombia-reports-normal-operations-at-border-crossings-with-venezuela/), [CNN 07/01/2025](https://edition.cnn.com/world/live-news/trump-venezuela-oil-greenland-07-01-26), [NYT 03/01/2025](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/03/world/americas/us-venezuela-tensions-timeline.html), [CFR accessed 07/01/2025](https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/instability-venezuela), [UN 06/01/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/01/1166708))



UPDATE 28/11/2025
The US Government has designated the so‑called Cartel de los Soles as an international terrorist entity, granting the Trump administration expanded economic and legal instruments to increase pressure on Venezuela and potentially pursue armed action against individuals associated with the group. Shortly thereafter, President Donald Trump signalled a shift in US operations from primarily maritime interdiction in the Caribbean Sea to possible on‑land actions inside Venezuela. This prompted the Maduro administration to place the armed forces on alert while simultaneously leaving open a diplomatic track, in which any easing of US pressure appears tied to Nicolás Maduro’s departure from power and the prospect of exile options, including in countries such as Türkiye.
Public statements from both Washington and Caracas, as well as third‑party actors such as Türkiye, suggest that channels for dialogue remain nominally open and that some parties are encouraging a negotiated de‑escalation between the US and Venezuela. That said, there is currently no clear evidence of formal negotiations aimed at reducing tensions or reaching a political settlement, and reports of talks or proposals largely stem from isolated offers, indirect contacts, or unconfirmed media leaks rather than an established negotiation process.
([The Conversation 24/11/2025](https://theconversation.com/por-que-la-presion-de-trump-sobre-venezuela-no-tiene-precedentes-y-podria-llevar-a-una-intervencion-militar-268954), [CNN 24/11/2025](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2025/11/24/eeuu/gobierno-trump-designa-maduro-venezuela-organizacion-terrorista-extranjera-trax), [CNN 27/11/2025](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/11/27/americas/maduro-venezuela-military-caribbean-trump-intl-latam-vis), [DW 28/11/2025](https://www.dw.com/es/maduro-ordena-a-la-fuerza-a%C3%A9rea-estar-lista-para-defender-venezuela/a-74933077), [TWP 27/11/2025](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/11/27/venezuela-turkey-maduro-erdogan-exile/))

R1059.title: Tensions between the military and political components in Sudan’s transitional government result in social unrest and increased access constraints for humanitarian organisations
R1059.what_happened: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed th...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed the pipeline that carries oil to Khartoum. The pipeline was reopened after two days, following a meeting with government officials. In response, Arab tribes in Kassala state protested against the Beja tribes’ blocking of roads and ports. The Beja tribes continued to block Red Sea ports and highways connecting eastern Sudan with the rest of the country until mid-October 2021. The Government warned that the country was running out of life-saving medicines, fuel, and wheat stocks.

R1045.title: El Niño in Zimbabwe increases the needs of those already affected by drought, cyclones, disease outbreaks, and protracted economic instability
R1045.what_happened: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Fr...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño was expected to cause below-average rainfall during the 2023–2024 agricultural season. This materialised, with Zimbabwe experiencing prolonged dry conditions and drought during its critical farming period (November 2023 to March 2024). These weather conditions directly impacted the country’s ability to grow and harvest staple crops
evolution.impact_materialisation: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Freddy, disease outbreaks, and economic instability, are now facing heightened humanitarian needs. The prolonged dry conditions have also caused severe water shortages, exacerbating WASH challenges and contributing to a resurgence of waterborne diseases such as cholera. These compounded effects have placed immense strain on nutrition, health, and protection services, prompting the government to declare a national disaster in early 2025 and appeal for international support to address the worsening crisis.

R1045.title: Consecutive below-average rains amid expected La Niña conditions in northern and central Somalia deepen drought Impacts
R1045.what_happened: The anticipated humanitarian impacts materialised, as prolonged drought severely affected livelihoods, food security, water availability, and displacement patterns. In January 2026, drought affected an estimated 4.61 million people, with at least 120...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The climate hazard partially materialised, although not through the initially anticipated La Niña mechanism. Instead of La Niña-driven below-average Deyr rainfall, Somalia experienced a continuation of drought conditions following failed 2025 Deyr rains and an unusually harsh Jilaal season. By early 2026, drought conditions had intensified, with forecasts indicating delayed and uneven recovery during the 2026 Gu season. The shift towards El Niño later in 2026 changed the expected hazard profile from prolonged drought to a potential drought-to-flood transition, particularly in the Juba and Shabelle River Basins.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The anticipated humanitarian impacts materialised, as prolonged drought severely affected livelihoods, food security, water availability, and displacement patterns. In January 2026, drought affected an estimated 4.61 million people, with at least 120,000 displaced between September–December 2025. More than 170 boreholes and shallow wells were reported non-functional, while drought conditions contributed to widespread Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity, with some areas at risk of Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5). Livestock losses, reduced agricultural production, water shortages, and displacement increased humanitarian needs, particularly in central and southern Somalia.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 09/06/2026
The developing El Niño, forecast to intensify from mid-2026, raises the prospect of a significant shift in Somalia's hazard profile later in the year. El Niño is expected to be more intense than the 2023 event, with the main risk shifting from drought to flooding along the Juba and Shabelle rivers as the October–December Deyr season approaches. There is also a possibility of riverine flooding before El Niño's arrival, driven by above-normal Kiremt rains in the Ethiopian highlands between June–September. Communities already severely weakened by consecutive drought seasons – with depleted livestock, exhausted water infrastructure, and eroded coping capacity – are unlikely to have recovered before potential flooding arrives, raising the risk that a drought-to-flood transition will deepen displacement and disease burdens across southern and central Somalia.
([FAO 30/04/2026](https://www.fao.org/somalia/news/details/somalia-faces-a-triple-threat-of-drought--middle-east-conflict-and-predicted-el-ni%C3%B1o-flooding--fao-warns/en), [OCHA 06/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-2025-2026-drought-emergency-situation-report-no-5-6-april-2026), [ICPAC 19/05/2026] https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/))


UPDATE 02/04/2026
Since March 2026, the drought risk has remained very high and its impacts have further intensified, even though the Deyr season has ended. Failed 2025 Deyr rains and an atypically harsh Jilaal have driven widespread Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes, with some areas at risk of Catastrophe/Famine (IPC Phase 5), alongside increasing drought‑related displacement and livestock losses. Millions are facing severe food insecurity and water shortages, with coping capacity eroded after consecutive poor seasons. Gu 2026 forecasts point to a delayed onset and high temperature stress, with only partial and uneven rainfall recovery expected, suggesting that acute needs will remain elevated through at least mid‑2026, particularly in central and southern Somalia. ([FEWS NET 10/02/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/somalia/key-message-update/january-2026), [OCHA 09/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-2025-2026-drought-emergency-situation-report-no-4), [FAO 03/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/swalim-update-somalia-gu-2026-climate-outlook-issued-3-march-2026), [MoECC 16/02/2026](https://moecc.gov.so/somalia-releases-gu-2026-seasonal-climate-outlook-highlighting-increased-rainfall-and-flood-risks/))


UPDATE 28/01/2026
Drought has intensified over the past month, driven by worsening climatic conditions and increasing humanitarian impacts. Prolonged dry conditions have affected an estimated 4.61 million people as of January, with at least 120,000 people displaced between September and December, particularly in central and Lower Somalia. Critical water infrastructure continues to fail, with over 170 boreholes and shallow wells reported non-functional, further reducing access to safe water. The drought has also disrupted basic services, forcing approximately 75,000 students to drop out of school. The January–March 2026 Jilaal dry season is expected to aggravate water scarcity, abnormal livestock movements and rising livestock mortality, likely worsening acute food insecurity. Continued displacement towards urban centres and IDP sites is expected, increasing pressure on already fragile living conditions, access to services and livelihood opportunities.([OCHA 21/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-2025-drought-emergency-situation-report-no-2-21-december-2025), [OCHA 27/01/2026] (https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026))


30/10/2025
Forecast remains concerning about the dry situation in Somalia. Dry conditions driven by below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures are expected to worsen in already drought-affected northern regions, while recovery in the south following the 2025 Gu and Hagaa rains may stall owing to poor Deyr performance. There is an increased likelihood (around 55%) of drier-than-normal conditions across southern and central Somalia and coastal areas of Somaliland. A moderate likelihood (about 45%) of dry conditions is also forecast for Somaliland and central Puntland. In the northeast, conditions remain uncertain, but heat stress risks are expected to stay high. Overall, drought conditions in Somaliland and Puntland (northern Somalia) are likely to deteriorate further. ([FAO 06/10/2025](https://faoswalim.org/resources/site_files/Somalia_climate_outlook_for_the_2025_deyr_season.pdf))

R1045.title: La Niña in Afghanistan worsens drought and leads to widespread agricultural losses, water scarcity, and acute food insecurity in 2026
R1045.what_happened: The latest food insecurity projections indicate that over 17.4 million people are facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food security levels between November 2025 and March 2026, reflecting declining crop yields and rural incomes. Spring water availab...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: By March–April 2026, the climate-driven risk in Afghanistan has materialised into a worsening drought and food security crisis. Persistent La Niña conditions since late 2025 have resulted in below-average snowfall and rainfall and above-average temperatures, reducing water availability and damaging agricultural production. Additionally, spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt. ([Fews Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 03/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content))
evolution.impact_materialisation: The latest food insecurity projections indicate that over 17.4 million people are facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food security levels between November 2025 and March 2026, reflecting declining crop yields and rural incomes. Spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt, limiting irrigation, pasture growth, and livestock productivity. Fodder shortages are increasingly affecting pastoral households. At the same time, the return of over 2 million Afghans from Iran and Pakistan continues to strain food systems and water resources, particularly in border provinces. ([FEWS Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 06/04/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025))
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 31/03/2026
As of March 2026, Afghanistan faces escalating climate-driven risks linked to ongoing La Niña conditions that began in October 2025. Below-average snowfall and rainfall, combined with above-normal temperatures, are reinforcing drought conditions nationwide. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions are particularly affected, with rising agricultural and hydrological drought risks. This follows four consecutive years (2022–2025) of below-average production and crop failures in key regions. Second-season crops in 2025, including rice, maize, and cotton, have been impacted, while reduced winter precipitation threatens 2026 wheat production. Limited snowmelt and weakened river flows are expected to worsen water scarcity, constraining irrigation, pasture growth, and drinking water access. Pastoralist households face fodder shortages, reducing livestock productivity. Combined with earthquake impacts and large-scale population movements, these overlapping shocks are intensifying food insecurity, straining livelihoods, and overwhelming coping capacities ahead of the 2026 lean season. ([Fews Net 04/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-favorable-soil-moisture-conditions-are-beneficial-spring-wheat-planting-march-3-2026), [AP News 30/03/2026](https://apnews.com/article/weather-floods-afghanistan-storm-landslide-e6be89ef89f32f5d8c68f3380bdebbe7), [FAO 21/01/2026](https://media.un.org/unifeed/en/asset/d352/d3526668), [Reuters 03/03/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/un-warns-200000-more-afghan-children-face-acute-malnutrition-2026-2026-03-03/)    


UPDATE 09/02/2026
In February 2026, drought risk remains high across the country. Despite some improvements in western areas, multiple sources confirm the persistence of below-average winter precipitation, low snowpack, and above-average temperatures, continuing to place significant strain on water availability, agricultural production, and food systems. The 2025 wet season began significantly below average from October–November across most areas, leading to widespread deficits. Late rains, combined with low soil moisture from earlier months, disrupted rain-fed winter wheat planting, particularly in the north and northeast, and reduced the overall planted area. Between October 2025 and January 2026, southern provinces, especially Helmand and Kandahar, experienced the highest precipitation deficits of 30–60% below average. This is constraining irrigation supplies and increasing soil moisture stress ahead of the spring 2026 agricultural season.
The WFP estimates that 17.4 million people will face acute food insecurity through March 2026, including nearly five million malnourished women and children. These outcomes are driven in part by drought-related impacts on crops and rural livelihoods, compounded by economic shocks and large-scale returnee inflows. ([FEWS NET 02/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-january-precipitation-reduced-seasonal-deficits-benefiting-surface-and-groundwater-resources-february-2-2026), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025#:~:text=Some%20seasonal%20improvement%20is%20expected,levels%20of%20acute%20food%20insecurity.), [Crop Monitor 05/02/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [WFP accessed 09/02/2025](https://www.wfp.org/countries/afghanistan), [FAO 06/01/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/46600ceb-a104-4223-88e9-0ccfae273327/content))

R1071.title: Drought conditions due to the El Nino, high rice prices in the international market, and restrictions imposed by India on their rice exports worsen food insecurity outcomes
R1071.what_happened: Around 360,000 people (27% of the population) are estimated to face crisis or above levels of food insecurity (IPC 3 and above) in November 2023—April 2024. It is nearly 100,000 more than the projected figure for May—September 2023. Number of people...

evolution.hazard_materialisation:
Poverty, El Nino induced drought-like conditions, and high food prices were found to be among the primary drivers of food insecurity.

Unfavourable weather conditions including the current El Nino event, and shortfall in production of rice in the main rice producing and exporting countries, led to limited global rice availability.

Rice and maize are the two main staple foods in the country. Timor-Leste has high dependency on imported rice to meet their demand of rice. Price of imported rice was 30% higher in December 2023 compared to December 2022. Maize prices rose by 66% during the same period, and its production is expected to decrease in 2024 due to the impact of El Nino and fall armyworm infestations.
evolution.impact_materialisation:
Around 360,000 people (27% of the population) are estimated to face crisis or above levels of food insecurity (IPC 3 and above) in November 2023—April 2024. It is nearly 100,000 more than the projected figure for May—September 2023. Number of people facing emergency level food security (IPC 4) has more than doubled from 7,000 to around 18,600 in the same period. 

The El Nino is expected to have negative impacts on the national and regional rice and maize production in 2024, leading to limited food availability and increased food prices, and reducing agriculture-related livelihood opportunities and household food reserves. The situation is expected to worsen the food insecurity situation in the post-harvest season, May—September 2024, when food access and availability generally improves. The number of people facing crisis or above levels of food insecurity (IPC 3 and above) is projected to rise to 364,000.
