R1071.title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and flooding in Colombia cause widespread crop damage, landslides, waterborne diseases, and food insecurity and malnutrition
R1071.what_happened: From November 2025 to January 2026, heavy rains, floods, and landslides impacted 115,000 families, affected 24 of the country's 32 departments, and forced the closure of major roads in several departments across the country. This resulted in 600 repo...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: From November 2025 to January 2026, heavy rains, floods, and landslides impacted 115,000 families, affected 24 of the country's 32 departments, and forced the closure of major roads in several departments across the country. This resulted in 600 reported emergencies. The risk materialised both in impact and extent.
evolution.impact_materialisation: From November 2025 to January 2026, heavy rains, floods, and landslides impacted 115,000 families, affected 24 of the country's 32 departments, and forced the closure of major roads in several departments across the country. This resulted in 600 reported emergencies. The risk materialised both in impact and extent.
evolution.rationale_update:
Update 11/06/2026
Between January-June 2026, at least 600 rain-related emergencies have been reported in 24 of Colombia's 32 departments, affecting 155,000 families – five times more than in the first semester of 2025. Floods and rising river levels were concentrated particularly in the departments of Antioquia, Caldas, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Huila, and Valle del Cauca. The transition from La Niña to El Niño is expected by June, with El Niño reaching its peak in September. As a result, rainfall has already decreased, and above-average temperatures and below-average rainfall are expected in the coming months.
([Marsh 01/05/2026](https://www.marsh.com/es/services/climate-change-adaption/insights/climate-agenda-2026-el-nino-impact.html), [UNGRD 25/03/2026](https://portal.gestiondelriesgo.gov.co/Paginas/Noticias/2026/Asi-se-comportara-el-clima-en-Colombia-IDEAM-UNGRD-y-DIMAR-entregan-predicciones-y-recomendaciones.aspx), [WWF 13/02/2026](https://www.wwf.org.co/?399751/Lluvias-en-Colombia-2026), [El Tiempo 25/03/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/vida/medio-ambiente/emergencia-nacional-por-lluvias-hay-mas-de-155-000-familias-damnificadas-un-574-mas-que-el-ano-anterior-3542816)) 

UPDATE 30/04/2026
La Niña-associated heavy rainfall and flooding across Colombia appear to have subsided, with neutral conditions and average precipitation maintained throughout April. However, Colombia is now transitioning towards El Niño conditions, with a 60% probability of onset between May and June, rising to 90% between June and November. El Niño is typically associated with elevated temperatures, drought, heatwaves, and below-average rainfall — conditions that are in direct contrast to those produced by La Niña and that carry significant implications for agricultural production, water availability, and food security across already vulnerable communities in the months ahead. ([CPC 09/04/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc_Sp.shtml); [IDEAM 11/04/2026](https://www.ideam.gov.co/sala-de-prensa/noticia/ideam-y-minambiente-alertan-de-90-de-probabilidad-de-llegada-del-fenomeno-de-el-nino-para-septiembre#:~:text=Existe%20una%20probabilidad%20del%2061%25%20de%20que,en%20un%2090%25%20para%20septiembre%20de%202026.))


UPDATE 31/03/2026
Persistent La Niña-associated rainfall across Colombia has shown signs of easing throughout March, indicating a trend toward stabilization and a slight improvement in humanitarian conditions. By late February, more than half a million people across 22 departments had been affected by heavy rainfall since the start of 2026; however, heavy rain recorded during March does not seem to have created climatic events of comparable magnitude or significantly increased the number of people affected. Only in the department of Huila, in southern Colombia, was heavy rainfall recorded, but without resulting in new people affected.
Looking ahead, conditions are expected to shift from above-average rainfall to below-average precipitation, signaling a move toward seasonal drought across affected areas. This poses an additional concern for food production, given that tens of hectares of crops and thousands of animals had already been lost due to the previous flooding — leaving agricultural communities with significantly reduced capacity to recover and sustain livelihoods in the coming months. ([ECHO 10/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/colombia-severe-weather-ideam-meteo-colombia-media-echo-daily-flash-10-march-2026?_gl=1*1hbd590*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzU0NzgyNTMkbzQkZzEkdDE3NzU0NzgzODckajU5JGwwJGgw); [ECHO 06/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/colombia-floods-and-landslides-update-dg-echo-wfp-ungrd-un-ocha-ideam-echo-daily-flash-6-march-2026?_gl=1*c11nxx*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzU0NzgyNTMkbzQkZzEkdDE3NzU0Nzg0MTMkajMzJGwwJGgw); [Infobae 25/03/2026](https://www.infobae.com/colombia/2026/03/26/colombia-pasaria-de-inundaciones-a-sequia-en-2026-las-autoridades-lanzan-alerta-por-la-llegada-de-el-nino/)) 


UPDATE 27/02/2026
Persistent heavy rainfall associated with La Niña conditions triggered widespread landslides and flooding across Colombia in January and February 2026, affecting nearly 252,000 individuals across 22 of the country's 32 departments and compounding an already deteriorating humanitarian situation. Córdoba remains the most critically affected department, accounting for 66% of the national caseload, with the majority of its territory inundated. In La Guajira, flooding had reached approximately 32,000 people by early February; the department's capital water network is at risk of overflow, further aggravating chronic drinking water shortages that disproportionately impact Indigenous communities in the area.
Damage to critical infrastructure — including water systems, schools, healthcare facilities, and housing — has been reported across Antioquia, Cauca, Chocó, Córdoba, La Guajira, Nariño, and Sucre. The destruction of road networks continues to constrain both national and humanitarian response capacities, deepening pre-existing vulnerabilities among affected populations. With La Niña conditions expected to persist for March, the situation is expected to deteriorate further with more floods, increasing the risk of compounding impacts on communities already exposed to climatic shocks since late 2025. ([Copernicus Accessed 27/02/2026](https://mapping.emergency.copernicus.eu/activations/EMSR865/reporting/); [OCHA 20/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/latinoamerica-y-el-caribe-resumen-de-situacion-semanal-al-20-de-febrero-2026?_gl=1*1a04k3b*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzE4NDY0NjUkbzcyJGcxJHQxNzcxODQ2Njk1JGo2MCRsMCRoMA); [OCHA Emergency Tracker Accessed 23/02/2026](https://colombia-emergency-response-tracker.consorcioevidem.org/))

R1044.title: El Niño in Zimbabwe increases the needs of those already affected by drought, cyclones, disease outbreaks, and protracted economic instability
R1044.what_happened: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Fr...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño was expected to cause below-average rainfall during the 2023–2024 agricultural season. This materialised, with Zimbabwe experiencing prolonged dry conditions and drought during its critical farming period (November 2023 to March 2024). These weather conditions directly impacted the country’s ability to grow and harvest staple crops
evolution.impact_materialisation: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Freddy, disease outbreaks, and economic instability, are now facing heightened humanitarian needs. The prolonged dry conditions have also caused severe water shortages, exacerbating WASH challenges and contributing to a resurgence of waterborne diseases such as cholera. These compounded effects have placed immense strain on nutrition, health, and protection services, prompting the government to declare a national disaster in early 2025 and appeal for international support to address the worsening crisis.

R1044.title: El Niño-driven above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation cause widespread drought in the Central American Dry Corridor (El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras), increasing food and health needs
R1044.what_happened: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by fo...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño conditions and above-average temperatures are affecting Central America’s Dry Corridor, with particularly strong temperature evidence in El Salvador and Guatemala. El Niño conditions are forecast to strengthen during September–November, with a peak expected towards the end of 2026. In Honduras, there was a 100% probability of El Niño occurring during August–October, intensifying the mid-summer dry spell in late July and August and prompting drought alerts in 13 departments. In El Salvador, 14 temperature records were set in August, with temperatures reaching 43.9° C in Santa Rosa de Lima (La Unión Norte). Seasonal rainfall for August–November was forecast at 831.6mm, below the 939.0mm average, and a national red alert was declared on 25 August. In Guatemala, high temperatures caused rapid soil moisture loss, particularly in the Dry Corridor, where August rainfall reached only 5–25% of normal levels. In the Dry Corridor, farmers reported crop losses exceeding 50%, and some subsistence farmers reported losses of backyard poultry. No temperature data is available for Honduras, and the reported conditions do not establish direct attribution of specific impacts to El Niño. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))
evolution.impact_materialisation: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by food security and nutrition (622,000), health (617,000), and protection (400,000, including 80,000 targeted). Nationally, 1.88 million people are projected to face IPC 3 or worse between August–October. In Guatemala, the poorest households are likely to reduce food consumption and sell productive assets. Across 354 communities in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% had maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. Agricultural employment has contracted sharply, particularly in El Salvador. Dehydration, child labour, family separation, and gender-based violence are additional anticipated concerns, although their impacts remain unquantified. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 21/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026)).
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 02/10/2026
Food insecurity in Central America’s Dry Corridor is deepening as primera crop losses are confirmed and El Niño strengthens. In Honduras, 1.88 million people (18% of the analysed population) are projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between August–October, around 108,500 more than projected in March. Eight departments are classified in IPC 3. Over708,000 people in 103 red-alert municipalities could require assistance. In Guatemala, delayed planting is preventing the poorest households in the Dry Corridor, Alta Verapaz, and the Western Highlands from accessing primera harvests, which normally begin in September. These households are projected to face IPC 3 outcomes through September. In 354 assessed communities across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% have maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. A weak postrera harvest could prolong food needs into 2027. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))

UPDATE 02/09/2026
The risk of drought and elevated temperatures across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras has deteriorated during August 2026, as the impacts of the El Niño phenomenon continue to affect the Dry Corridor agricultural zone shared by the three countries. At least five million people across Honduras and Guatemala currently face the threat of food insecurity, driven in part by reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures linked to El Niño. In Guatemala, above-average temperatures and irregular rainfall in July 2026 have reduced food production in the departments of Alta Verapaz, Huehuetenango, Jalapa, Jutiapa, Quiché, and Zacapa. A similar situation has unfolded in Honduras, where communities across 75 municipalities were placed on yellow drought alert in August as a result of reduced rainfall linked to El Niño. A heat wave has also been affecting El Salvador since 11 August, with six weather stations recording heatwave conditions across the country. Historical temperature records have been broken at multiple stations, including San Francisco Gotera (40.6° C on 13 August) and San Andrés in La Libertad (40° C, the highest in 43 years). Temperatures in the eastern zone are forecast to reach between 38–41° C, with the heatwave expected to persist and potentially spread to additional areas before gradually decreasing from 20 August.
([NOAA13/08/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov), [FEWS NET 07/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala), [SWI/EFE 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch), [El Libertador 14/08/2026](https://ellibertador.hn/2026/08/14/viene-agua-75-municipios-hondurenos-alerta-amarilla-por-sequia-larga-48-verde-y-111-en-vigilancia/),[La Prensa Gráfica/EFE 09/08/2026](https://www.revistaeyn.com/centroamericaymundo/guatemala-el-nino-amenaza-con-dejar-sin-alimento-a-32-millones-de-personas-EA31648419), [El Salvador 14/08/2026](https://www.elsalvador.com/?p=1289063)) 


UPDATE 03/08/2026
The risk has deteriorated. El Niño weather patterns have begun to affect the Dry Corridor region in Central America, driving up temperatures and reducing rainfall by up to 50% compared to typical levels for the season that normally begins in June. In Guatemala, Alta Verapaz and Western Highlands regions have experienced irregular rainfall and elevated temperatures since June, resulting in reduced harvests and a decline in agricultural labour opportunities, which in turn have reduced household income for families dependent on seasonal agricultural employment. As a result, the number of people in need of food assistance in Guatemala is projected to reach up to 2.49 million by August. A similar impact is expected in Honduras, particularly in Choluteca region and along the Dry Corridor, where El Niño impacts have reduced agricultural production and labour demand, exposing 750,000 people to food insecurity by August. Erratic, below-average rainfall and high temperatures brought by El Niño have also affected the western and Dry Corridor areas of El Salvador, depleting food reserves among smallholder farmers and agricultural workers and diminishing their food purchasing capacity. That said, the number of people expected to face food insecurity needs in El Salvador is not projected to reach the same scale as in Guatemala. Compounding these impacts, food prices have risen across most of the Dry Corridor in all three countries, driven by a combination of reduced food supply, increased demand as agricultural households are forced to purchase food they would otherwise produce, and price increases linked to rising inflation. ([FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/es/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala/perspectiva-de-seguridad-alimentaria/junio-2026/print); [Fews Net 31/06/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/el-salvador/key-message-update/may-2026/print), [FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/honduras/food-security-outlook/june-2026/print), [NOA 11/07/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))


UPDATE 03/07/2026
The risk has deteriorated as El Niño weather patterns have begun to produce measurable humanitarian impacts across the Dry Corridor. In Guatemala, irregular rainfall has caused crops to dry out before harvest, forcing Indigenous communities to draw on food reserves or financial resources to meet their nutritional needs. In El Salvador, authorities have confirmed that the entire country, including Dry Corridor provinces, is already under El Niño influence, with below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures forecast for July 2026. The most recent manifestation was a 12-day heat wave that sustained abnormally elevated temperatures across the country. In Honduras, El Niño-associated drought, compounded by dependence on staple crops such as maize and beans, has already reduced both planting areas and harvest yields during the primary mid-year agricultural season.
These developments are unfolding across a region that is home to ten million people, of whom approximately 80% depend directly on agricultural production for their livelihoods. As El Niño conditions persist and drought intensifies, declining food production is expected to place severe pressure on subsistence farming households in the Dry Corridor and all others across the three countries who rely on the market purchase of staple crops to meet their daily food needs. ([Canal 26 YouTube 05/06/2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yzz6fBOKmU0), [SWI 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/gobierno-de-el-salvador-confirma-influencia-de-el-ni%C3%B1o%2C-con-m%C3%A1s-calor-y-menos-lluvias/91707068), [Infobae 30/06/2026](https://www.infobae.com/el-salvador/2026/06/30/corredor-seco-en-alerta-sequias-por-el-nino-violencia-y-un-recorte-del-59-de-la-ayuda-empujan-a-guatemala-y-honduras-al-limite/), [NOAA 11/06/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))

R1046.title: El Niño in Zimbabwe increases the needs of those already affected by drought, cyclones, disease outbreaks, and protracted economic instability
R1046.what_happened: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Fr...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño was expected to cause below-average rainfall during the 2023–2024 agricultural season. This materialised, with Zimbabwe experiencing prolonged dry conditions and drought during its critical farming period (November 2023 to March 2024). These weather conditions directly impacted the country’s ability to grow and harvest staple crops
evolution.impact_materialisation: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Freddy, disease outbreaks, and economic instability, are now facing heightened humanitarian needs. The prolonged dry conditions have also caused severe water shortages, exacerbating WASH challenges and contributing to a resurgence of waterborne diseases such as cholera. These compounded effects have placed immense strain on nutrition, health, and protection services, prompting the government to declare a national disaster in early 2025 and appeal for international support to address the worsening crisis.

R1046.title: El Niño-driven above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation cause widespread drought in the Central American Dry Corridor (El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras), increasing food and health needs
R1046.what_happened: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by fo...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño conditions and above-average temperatures are affecting Central America’s Dry Corridor, with particularly strong temperature evidence in El Salvador and Guatemala. El Niño conditions are forecast to strengthen during September–November, with a peak expected towards the end of 2026. In Honduras, there was a 100% probability of El Niño occurring during August–October, intensifying the mid-summer dry spell in late July and August and prompting drought alerts in 13 departments. In El Salvador, 14 temperature records were set in August, with temperatures reaching 43.9° C in Santa Rosa de Lima (La Unión Norte). Seasonal rainfall for August–November was forecast at 831.6mm, below the 939.0mm average, and a national red alert was declared on 25 August. In Guatemala, high temperatures caused rapid soil moisture loss, particularly in the Dry Corridor, where August rainfall reached only 5–25% of normal levels. In the Dry Corridor, farmers reported crop losses exceeding 50%, and some subsistence farmers reported losses of backyard poultry. No temperature data is available for Honduras, and the reported conditions do not establish direct attribution of specific impacts to El Niño. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))
evolution.impact_materialisation: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by food security and nutrition (622,000), health (617,000), and protection (400,000, including 80,000 targeted). Nationally, 1.88 million people are projected to face IPC 3 or worse between August–October. In Guatemala, the poorest households are likely to reduce food consumption and sell productive assets. Across 354 communities in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% had maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. Agricultural employment has contracted sharply, particularly in El Salvador. Dehydration, child labour, family separation, and gender-based violence are additional anticipated concerns, although their impacts remain unquantified. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 21/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026)).
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 02/10/2026
Food insecurity in Central America’s Dry Corridor is deepening as primera crop losses are confirmed and El Niño strengthens. In Honduras, 1.88 million people (18% of the analysed population) are projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between August–October, around 108,500 more than projected in March. Eight departments are classified in IPC 3. Over708,000 people in 103 red-alert municipalities could require assistance. In Guatemala, delayed planting is preventing the poorest households in the Dry Corridor, Alta Verapaz, and the Western Highlands from accessing primera harvests, which normally begin in September. These households are projected to face IPC 3 outcomes through September. In 354 assessed communities across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% have maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. A weak postrera harvest could prolong food needs into 2027. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))

UPDATE 02/09/2026
The risk of drought and elevated temperatures across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras has deteriorated during August 2026, as the impacts of the El Niño phenomenon continue to affect the Dry Corridor agricultural zone shared by the three countries. At least five million people across Honduras and Guatemala currently face the threat of food insecurity, driven in part by reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures linked to El Niño. In Guatemala, above-average temperatures and irregular rainfall in July 2026 have reduced food production in the departments of Alta Verapaz, Huehuetenango, Jalapa, Jutiapa, Quiché, and Zacapa. A similar situation has unfolded in Honduras, where communities across 75 municipalities were placed on yellow drought alert in August as a result of reduced rainfall linked to El Niño. A heat wave has also been affecting El Salvador since 11 August, with six weather stations recording heatwave conditions across the country. Historical temperature records have been broken at multiple stations, including San Francisco Gotera (40.6° C on 13 August) and San Andrés in La Libertad (40° C, the highest in 43 years). Temperatures in the eastern zone are forecast to reach between 38–41° C, with the heatwave expected to persist and potentially spread to additional areas before gradually decreasing from 20 August.
([NOAA13/08/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov), [FEWS NET 07/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala), [SWI/EFE 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch), [El Libertador 14/08/2026](https://ellibertador.hn/2026/08/14/viene-agua-75-municipios-hondurenos-alerta-amarilla-por-sequia-larga-48-verde-y-111-en-vigilancia/),[La Prensa Gráfica/EFE 09/08/2026](https://www.revistaeyn.com/centroamericaymundo/guatemala-el-nino-amenaza-con-dejar-sin-alimento-a-32-millones-de-personas-EA31648419), [El Salvador 14/08/2026](https://www.elsalvador.com/?p=1289063)) 


UPDATE 03/08/2026
The risk has deteriorated. El Niño weather patterns have begun to affect the Dry Corridor region in Central America, driving up temperatures and reducing rainfall by up to 50% compared to typical levels for the season that normally begins in June. In Guatemala, Alta Verapaz and Western Highlands regions have experienced irregular rainfall and elevated temperatures since June, resulting in reduced harvests and a decline in agricultural labour opportunities, which in turn have reduced household income for families dependent on seasonal agricultural employment. As a result, the number of people in need of food assistance in Guatemala is projected to reach up to 2.49 million by August. A similar impact is expected in Honduras, particularly in Choluteca region and along the Dry Corridor, where El Niño impacts have reduced agricultural production and labour demand, exposing 750,000 people to food insecurity by August. Erratic, below-average rainfall and high temperatures brought by El Niño have also affected the western and Dry Corridor areas of El Salvador, depleting food reserves among smallholder farmers and agricultural workers and diminishing their food purchasing capacity. That said, the number of people expected to face food insecurity needs in El Salvador is not projected to reach the same scale as in Guatemala. Compounding these impacts, food prices have risen across most of the Dry Corridor in all three countries, driven by a combination of reduced food supply, increased demand as agricultural households are forced to purchase food they would otherwise produce, and price increases linked to rising inflation. ([FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/es/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala/perspectiva-de-seguridad-alimentaria/junio-2026/print); [Fews Net 31/06/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/el-salvador/key-message-update/may-2026/print), [FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/honduras/food-security-outlook/june-2026/print), [NOA 11/07/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))


UPDATE 03/07/2026
The risk has deteriorated as El Niño weather patterns have begun to produce measurable humanitarian impacts across the Dry Corridor. In Guatemala, irregular rainfall has caused crops to dry out before harvest, forcing Indigenous communities to draw on food reserves or financial resources to meet their nutritional needs. In El Salvador, authorities have confirmed that the entire country, including Dry Corridor provinces, is already under El Niño influence, with below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures forecast for July 2026. The most recent manifestation was a 12-day heat wave that sustained abnormally elevated temperatures across the country. In Honduras, El Niño-associated drought, compounded by dependence on staple crops such as maize and beans, has already reduced both planting areas and harvest yields during the primary mid-year agricultural season.
These developments are unfolding across a region that is home to ten million people, of whom approximately 80% depend directly on agricultural production for their livelihoods. As El Niño conditions persist and drought intensifies, declining food production is expected to place severe pressure on subsistence farming households in the Dry Corridor and all others across the three countries who rely on the market purchase of staple crops to meet their daily food needs. ([Canal 26 YouTube 05/06/2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yzz6fBOKmU0), [SWI 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/gobierno-de-el-salvador-confirma-influencia-de-el-ni%C3%B1o%2C-con-m%C3%A1s-calor-y-menos-lluvias/91707068), [Infobae 30/06/2026](https://www.infobae.com/el-salvador/2026/06/30/corredor-seco-en-alerta-sequias-por-el-nino-violencia-y-un-recorte-del-59-de-la-ayuda-empujan-a-guatemala-y-honduras-al-limite/), [NOAA 11/06/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))

R1046.title: La Niña in Afghanistan worsens drought and leads to widespread agricultural losses, water scarcity, and acute food insecurity in 2026
R1046.what_happened: The latest food insecurity projections indicate that over 17.4 million people are facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food security levels between November 2025 and March 2026, reflecting declining crop yields and rural incomes. Spring water availab...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: By March–April 2026, the climate-driven risk in Afghanistan has materialised into a worsening drought and food security crisis. Persistent La Niña conditions since late 2025 have resulted in below-average snowfall and rainfall and above-average temperatures, reducing water availability and damaging agricultural production. Additionally, spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt. ([Fews Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 03/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content))
evolution.impact_materialisation: The latest food insecurity projections indicate that over 17.4 million people are facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food security levels between November 2025 and March 2026, reflecting declining crop yields and rural incomes. Spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt, limiting irrigation, pasture growth, and livestock productivity. Fodder shortages are increasingly affecting pastoral households. At the same time, the return of over 2 million Afghans from Iran and Pakistan continues to strain food systems and water resources, particularly in border provinces. ([FEWS Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 06/04/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025))
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 31/03/2026
As of March 2026, Afghanistan faces escalating climate-driven risks linked to ongoing La Niña conditions that began in October 2025. Below-average snowfall and rainfall, combined with above-normal temperatures, are reinforcing drought conditions nationwide. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions are particularly affected, with rising agricultural and hydrological drought risks. This follows four consecutive years (2022–2025) of below-average production and crop failures in key regions. Second-season crops in 2025, including rice, maize, and cotton, have been impacted, while reduced winter precipitation threatens 2026 wheat production. Limited snowmelt and weakened river flows are expected to worsen water scarcity, constraining irrigation, pasture growth, and drinking water access. Pastoralist households face fodder shortages, reducing livestock productivity. Combined with earthquake impacts and large-scale population movements, these overlapping shocks are intensifying food insecurity, straining livelihoods, and overwhelming coping capacities ahead of the 2026 lean season. ([Fews Net 04/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-favorable-soil-moisture-conditions-are-beneficial-spring-wheat-planting-march-3-2026), [AP News 30/03/2026](https://apnews.com/article/weather-floods-afghanistan-storm-landslide-e6be89ef89f32f5d8c68f3380bdebbe7), [FAO 21/01/2026](https://media.un.org/unifeed/en/asset/d352/d3526668), [Reuters 03/03/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/un-warns-200000-more-afghan-children-face-acute-malnutrition-2026-2026-03-03/)    


UPDATE 09/02/2026
In February 2026, drought risk remains high across the country. Despite some improvements in western areas, multiple sources confirm the persistence of below-average winter precipitation, low snowpack, and above-average temperatures, continuing to place significant strain on water availability, agricultural production, and food systems. The 2025 wet season began significantly below average from October–November across most areas, leading to widespread deficits. Late rains, combined with low soil moisture from earlier months, disrupted rain-fed winter wheat planting, particularly in the north and northeast, and reduced the overall planted area. Between October 2025 and January 2026, southern provinces, especially Helmand and Kandahar, experienced the highest precipitation deficits of 30–60% below average. This is constraining irrigation supplies and increasing soil moisture stress ahead of the spring 2026 agricultural season.
The WFP estimates that 17.4 million people will face acute food insecurity through March 2026, including nearly five million malnourished women and children. These outcomes are driven in part by drought-related impacts on crops and rural livelihoods, compounded by economic shocks and large-scale returnee inflows. ([FEWS NET 02/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-january-precipitation-reduced-seasonal-deficits-benefiting-surface-and-groundwater-resources-february-2-2026), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025#:~:text=Some%20seasonal%20improvement%20is%20expected,levels%20of%20acute%20food%20insecurity.), [Crop Monitor 05/02/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [WFP accessed 09/02/2025](https://www.wfp.org/countries/afghanistan), [FAO 06/01/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/46600ceb-a104-4223-88e9-0ccfae273327/content))

R1042.title: Failure of essential services owing to the blockade in Mali leads to civil unrest and destabilisation and aggravates needs
R1042.what_happened: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several region...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: JNIM's blockade strategy expanded beyond northern and central Mali into southern and western regions, targeting fuel convoys, transport corridors, and economic infrastructure. The blockade persisted throughout the monitoring period despite temporary fluctuations in fuel availability and continued to disrupt national supply chains and state control over key transport routes.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several regions. While large-scale civil unrest did not materialise, the blockade contributed to worsening humanitarian conditions, weakened state authority, and increased insecurity. Ongoing blockade-related dynamics are now captured under the new Mali risk on coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 27/04/2026
The risk remains high and increasingly volatile. While there were indications of a partial easing in the intensity of the fuel blockade earlier in April 2026, recent large-scale coordinated attacks across multiple cities highlight a renewed deterioration in the security environment. Attacks targeting key locations, including Kati near Bamako, and the reported death of the Minister of Defence underscore the extent of armed groups’ operational reach. These developments are likely to further undermine the State’s ability to secure key transport corridors and ensure the continuity of fuel supply, which remains heavily dependent on military-escorted convoys. The reported loss of control over areas such as Kidal and the withdrawal of allied forces also point to weakening state authority in strategic regions. As a result, the risk of renewed disruptions to fuel supply and essential services remains high. Combined with continued fuel price increases and inflationary pressures, this may further constrain access to electricity, healthcare, and markets, while increasing the likelihood of social tensions. Overall, recent events suggest that earlier improvements were fragile and that the structural drivers of the risk remain firmly in place. ([RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [RFI 02/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260402-mali-autorit%C3%A9s-accusent-des-entreprises-utiliser-crise-carburant-pour-gonfler-leurs-prix), [BBC 24/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/afrique/articles/cyv1rpn4753o), [Ledjely 01/04/2026](https://ledjely.com/2026/04/01/mali-la-hausse-du-carburant-fait-craindre-une-spirale-des-prix/), [Timbuktu Institute 17/04/2026](https://timbuktu-institute.org/index.php/toutes-l-actualites/item/1509-le-mali-entre-chocs-externes-et-defis-internes))


UPDATE 30/03/2026
The risk has slightly deteriorated, with more fuel shortages reported. On 28 March 2026, the Government of Mali raised diesel prices by nearly 30% and petrol prices by 13% in response to supply disruptions by the Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin blockade. The heightened impacts of the fuel shortages increase the likelihood of civil unrest. On 25 March, diesel shortages in Bamako intensified as limited fuel imports were further redirected to support electricity generation during a heat wave. Several fuel stations ran out of diesel, leading to long queues at remaining supply points and disrupting urban mobility. At least 100 public transport vehicles were taken out of service, while construction-related transport (e.g. sand and gravel trucks) halted. ([TRT 10/03/2026](https://www.trtafrika.com/article/27f0213a3997), [Bloomberg 28/03/2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-28/mali-raises-petrol-diesel-prices-and-cuts-some-fuel-subsidies))


UPDATE 26/02/2026
Since January, the risk linked to the fuel blockade and related insecurity has remained high and volatile, with continued attacks despite temporary supply improvements in Bamako. While fuel availability in the capital improved in early February, the broader trend points to sustained operational disruption and geographic expansion of insecurity.  Key developments include renewed large-scale JNIM attacks on fuel convoys near Kayes, leading to the killing of drivers and military escorts and prompting a nationwide transport strike on 9 February. In central Mali, state forces conducted airstrikes in Macina (Ségou Region) following reported insurgent activity in Sikasso, while in Kidal region, a convoy was targeted by both JNIM and Azawad Liberation Front elements, suggesting overlapping armed actor pressure in the north. Continued road blockades affecting multiple localities and persistent electricity shortages (6–8 hours per day in Bamako) indicate structural fragility. In the short to medium term, continued convoy insecurity and transport disruptions risk renewed fuel shortages, rising prices, reduced market access, and further constraints on electricity supply, livelihoods, and humanitarian access, particularly outside the capital. ([DW 10/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/fr/focus-sahel-plus-villes-sous-blocus-du-jnim-au-mali/a-75901357), [RFI 03/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260203-au-mali-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-plie-mais-ne-rompt-pas), [RFI 10/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260210-mali-cibles-d-attaques-jihadistes-des-chauffeurs-routiers-appellent-%C3%A0-un-arr%C3%AAt-de-travail), [RFI 20/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260220-mali-une-frappe-de-drone-des-rebelles-du-fla-contre-l-arm%C3%A9e-fait-des-morts-des-deux-c%C3%B4t%C3%A9s)). 


UPDATE 02/02/2026
Since the previous update, the risk associated with the fuel blockade has remained elevated but volatile, with short-lived improvements followed by renewed disruption. While some fuel circulation has resumed intermittently, shortages persisted throughout January 2026, indicating neither clear escalation nor stabilisation. Key developments point to a broadening of the blockade’s scope. In Bamako, electricity supply remains limited to around five to seven hours per day, and fuel availability continues to be intermittent, with long queues and growing reliance on informal markets. In the southwest, Nioro du Sahel remains under a near-total blockade since early September 2025, with movement restrictions, reported abductions, and the increasing scarcity of food, medicines, fuel, and water. In parallel, attacks linked to Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin have expanded beyond fuel convoys to economic infrastructure, including mid-January 2026 attacks on industrial sites in Kayes and late January attacks on fuel convoys. Authorities have announced tighter fuel controls and reinforced escorts ahead of Ramadan, but continued incidents suggest a persistent risk of disruption to essential services, rising living costs, constrained access to markets, and increasing humanitarian needs in affected urban and blockaded areas. ([RFI 10/01/2026)[https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260110-mali-des-habitants-de-nioro-du-sahel-racontent-le-blocus-jihadiste-qui-dure-depuis-cinq-mois), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-la-fourniture-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-de-carburant-reste-tr%C3%A8s-insuffisante-les-bamakois-se-r%C3%A9signent), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-le-manque-de-carburant-%C3%A0-l-a%C3%A9roport-de-bamako-perturbe-certaines-liaisons), [RFI 16/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260116-mali-blocus-jihadiste-%C3%A0-nioro-du-sahel-la-situation-est-sous-contr%C3%B4le-selon-les-autorit%C3%A9s-de-transition), [RFI 12/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260112-mali-comment-et-pourquoi-des-jihadistes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-trois-sites-industriels-de-la-r%C3%A9gion-de-kayes), [RFI 02/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260202-au-mali-les-autorit%C3%A9s-veulent-s%C3%A9curiser-l-apprivisionnement-de-carburant-pour-le-mois-de-ramadan))


UPDATE 18/12/2025
Since early December, the JNIM has resumed attacks on fuel convoys after a temporary slowdown observed in late November. The initial lull allowed some fuel deliveries to reach Bamako and Mopti, briefly reducing shortages and restoring limited electricity and public services. However, renewed ambushes in Bougouni, Ouélessébougou, and Ségou, including the destruction of over 15 fuel tankers and the killing of drivers, have reinstated supply chain disruptions and public anxiety. In Bamako, queues at petrol stations have grown again, diesel has become scarce, and intermittent power cuts have returned. While 300 trucks were received ahead of the AES summit in mid-December, the improvement remains temporary. In Mopti and surrounding areas, fuel convoys have resumed under heavy military protection, but the quantities remain insufficient to meet the demand. Electricity has returned for around nine hours per day, and some economic activity has restarted, though fuel prices on the black market remain triple the official rate.  The blockade continues to affect humanitarian operations and access to essential services. In areas such as Koulikoro, Sikasso, and Koutiala, fuel scarcity persists, with limited electricity, inaccessible health services, and rising transport costs. The JNIM’s strategy has evolved beyond physical control, aiming to delegitimise the state through economic strangulation and selective violence. The group is reportedly consolidating control over rural areas by offering basic services (such as justice and security) under Islamic governance, gradually normalising its authority.

R1042.title: The escalation of political and armed conflict in Southwest state leads to large‑scale displacement and worsens humanitarian conditions

evolution.hazard_materialisation: On 30 March 2026, federal forces backed by allied clan militias entered Baidoa following weeks of escalating political tensions, engaging in brief but heavy clashes with Southwest State regional forces before assuming control of the city. Southwest State President Laftagareen resigned and fled to Kenya. Further clashes between federal forces and Laftagareen loyalists erupted on the outskirts of Baidoa in late May 2026. Elections in Southwest State are currently underway amid continued instability. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))
evolution.impact_materialisation: The clashes and prolonged fear of wider confrontation triggered pre-emptive mass displacement of over 50,000 people, predominantly women and children, from Baidoa towards Burhakaba, Hudur, Waajid, and surrounding areas. Three people were killed and five injured. Schools, hospitals, and maternal and child health centres were temporarily closed. Displaced populations faced heightened protection risks including overcrowding, inadequate shelter, and gender-based violence exposure, compounding already severe drought-related displacement and food insecurity across Bay and Bakool. Some families have begun returning, though conditions remain fragile. Broader risks related to the federal–state constitutional tensions are captured under the Somalia constitutional crisis risk. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))

R1042.title: The deployment of the regional military force leads to more displacement and increased humanitarian needs in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
R1042.what_happened: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian cri...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: In response to the escalating activities of armed groups, including the March 23 Movement (M23), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) dispatched the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF) in November 2022. This multinational force, comprising troops from Kenya, Burundi, South Sudan, and Uganda, was deployed to bring stability to the conflict-torn eastern regions of the DRC. However, the presence of the EACRF led to heightened clashes between military forces and various armed factions, exacerbating security challenges in the region. These clashes caused a large number of civilians to leave conflict zones, increasing the need for humanitarian aid in the region. The departure of the EACRF in December 2023 created a security gap that was swiftly taken advantage of by armed groups, further exacerbating instability.
evolution.impact_materialisation: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian crisis, with critical needs in areas such as shelter, food, water, sanitation, and medical care. The situation has been aggravated by the suspension of activities by numerous humanitarian organisations due to persistent insecurity.

R1047.title: La Niña-induced heavy rainfall and enhanced cyclonic activity from October–March in central and northern Mozambique increase flooding and displacement
R1047.what_happened: The impacts have also materialised. Persistent flooding since December 2025 has triggered expanded inundation across Manica, Nampula, Sofala, Tete, and Zambezia, leading to continued evacuation (with at least 112,800 displaced), localised infrastruct...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The La Niña‑induced hazard has fully materialised. Weak La Niña conditions persisted into the October 2025 to March 2026 rainy season, producing above‑average and prolonged rainfall across central and northern Mozambique. This resulted in repeated heavy rain events over already-saturated river basins, causing water in the Zambezi, Licungo, Pungoe, and Save Rivers to rise further and overflow. Cyclonic disturbances and low‑pressure systems in the Mozambique Channel intensified the hazard by generating short‑duration but high‑intensity rainfall, overwhelming drainage systems and weakening flood defences. The forecast hazard (excess rainfall, riverine flooding, and enhanced cyclone activity) transitioned into sustained hydrometeorological extremes, confirming full hazard materialisation.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The impacts have also materialised. Persistent flooding since December 2025 has triggered expanded inundation across Manica, Nampula, Sofala, Tete, and Zambezia, leading to continued evacuation (with at least 112,800 displaced), localised infrastructure damage, and crop losses. Saturated catchments and repeated flooding have disrupted community access, hindered service delivery, and contributed to worsening food insecurity by damaging or destroying agricultural fields. The strain on basic services has increased, particularly in low‑lying river basins and coastal districts, heightening risks of disease outbreaks by compromising water and sanitation systems. The situation has escalated from predicted impacts to tangible humanitarian consequences, confirming full impact materialisation.
evolution.rationale_update:
Update 30/01/2025
The risk of flooding and weather-induced displacement in Mozambique has intensified since December 2025 as La Niña–driven rainfall has translated into sustained, on-the-ground impacts. During January 2026, above-average rainfall persisted across central and northern provinces, with repeated heavy rain episodes falling on already saturated catchments. This has driven further rises in the Zambezi, Licungo, Pungue and Save rivers and expanded flooding in Zambézia, Sofala, Tete, Manica and Nampula.
Cyclonic disturbances and active low-pressure systems in the Mozambique Channel have acted as key aggravating factors, generating short-duration but high-intensity rainfall that has overwhelmed drainage systems and weakened flood defences. Localised infrastructure damage, crop losses and continued population displacement indicate an escalation from forecast risk to realised impact.
In the short to medium term, continued flooding through the remainder of the rainy season is likely to deepen humanitarian needs, disrupt access to affected communities, increase food insecurity due to crop destruction, and strain basic services, particularly in low-lying river basins and coastal districts.
([ECHO 29/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-severe-weather-and-floods-update-ingd-noaa-cpc-echo-daily-flash-29-january-2026), [ECHO 20/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-severe-weather-and-floods-update-ingd-copernicus-emsr-dg-echo-noaa-southern-africa-echo-daily-flash-20-january-2026), [UNFPA 19/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/unfpa-mozambique-heavy-rains-and-flooding-flash-update-19-january-2026), [IOM 19/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-heavy-rains-and-flooding-displacement-update-18-january-2026), [OCHA 18/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/flash-update-no3-heavy-rains-and-floods-central-and-southern-mozambique-18-january-2026))

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño was expected to cause below-average rainfall during the 2023–2024 agricultural season. This materialised, with Zimbabwe experiencing prolonged dry conditions and drought during its critical farming period (November 2023 to March 2024). These weather conditions directly impacted the country’s ability to grow and harvest staple crops
evolution.impact_materialisation: The impact of the El Niño-induced drought in Zimbabwe materialised, resulting in widespread crop failure and a sharp increase in food insecurity across the country. Millions of people, many already vulnerable due to previous shocks such as Cyclone Freddy, disease outbreaks, and economic instability, are now facing heightened humanitarian needs. R1047.title: El Niño-driven above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation cause widespread drought in the Central American Dry Corridor (El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras), increasing food and health needs
R1047.what_happened: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by fo...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: El Niño conditions and above-average temperatures are affecting Central America’s Dry Corridor, with particularly strong temperature evidence in El Salvador and Guatemala. El Niño conditions are forecast to strengthen during September–November, with a peak expected towards the end of 2026. In Honduras, there was a 100% probability of El Niño occurring during August–October, intensifying the mid-summer dry spell in late July and August and prompting drought alerts in 13 departments. In El Salvador, 14 temperature records were set in August, with temperatures reaching 43.9° C in Santa Rosa de Lima (La Unión Norte). Seasonal rainfall for August–November was forecast at 831.6mm, below the 939.0mm average, and a national red alert was declared on 25 August. In Guatemala, high temperatures caused rapid soil moisture loss, particularly in the Dry Corridor, where August rainfall reached only 5–25% of normal levels. In the Dry Corridor, farmers reported crop losses exceeding 50%, and some subsistence farmers reported losses of backyard poultry. No temperature data is available for Honduras, and the reported conditions do not establish direct attribution of specific impacts to El Niño. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))
evolution.impact_materialisation: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by food security and nutrition (622,000), health (617,000), and protection (400,000, including 80,000 targeted). Nationally, 1.88 million people are projected to face IPC 3 or worse between August–October. In Guatemala, the poorest households are likely to reduce food consumption and sell productive assets. Across 354 communities in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% had maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. Agricultural employment has contracted sharply, particularly in El Salvador. Dehydration, child labour, family separation, and gender-based violence are additional anticipated concerns, although their impacts remain unquantified. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 21/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026)).
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 02/10/2026
Food insecurity in Central America’s Dry Corridor is deepening as primera crop losses are confirmed and El Niño strengthens. In Honduras, 1.88 million people (18% of the analysed population) are projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between August–October, around 108,500 more than projected in March. Eight departments are classified in IPC 3. Over708,000 people in 103 red-alert municipalities could require assistance. In Guatemala, delayed planting is preventing the poorest households in the Dry Corridor, Alta Verapaz, and the Western Highlands from accessing primera harvests, which normally begin in September. These households are projected to face IPC 3 outcomes through September. In 354 assessed communities across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% have maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. A weak postrera harvest could prolong food needs into 2027. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))

UPDATE 02/09/2026
The risk of drought and elevated temperatures across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras has deteriorated during August 2026, as the impacts of the El Niño phenomenon continue to affect the Dry Corridor agricultural zone shared by the three countries. At least five million people across Honduras and Guatemala currently face the threat of food insecurity, driven in part by reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures linked to El Niño. In Guatemala, above-average temperatures and irregular rainfall in July 2026 have reduced food production in the departments of Alta Verapaz, Huehuetenango, Jalapa, Jutiapa, Quiché, and Zacapa. A similar situation has unfolded in Honduras, where communities across 75 municipalities were placed on yellow drought alert in August as a result of reduced rainfall linked to El Niño. A heat wave has also been affecting El Salvador since 11 August, with six weather stations recording heatwave conditions across the country. Historical temperature records have been broken at multiple stations, including San Francisco Gotera (40.6° C on 13 August) and San Andrés in La Libertad (40° C, the highest in 43 years). Temperatures in the eastern zone are forecast to reach between 38–41° C, with the heatwave expected to persist and potentially spread to additional areas before gradually decreasing from 20 August.
([NOAA13/08/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov), [FEWS NET 07/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala), [SWI/EFE 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch), [El Libertador 14/08/2026](https://ellibertador.hn/2026/08/14/viene-agua-75-municipios-hondurenos-alerta-amarilla-por-sequia-larga-48-verde-y-111-en-vigilancia/),[La Prensa Gráfica/EFE 09/08/2026](https://www.revistaeyn.com/centroamericaymundo/guatemala-el-nino-amenaza-con-dejar-sin-alimento-a-32-millones-de-personas-EA31648419), [El Salvador 14/08/2026](https://www.elsalvador.com/?p=1289063)) 


UPDATE 03/08/2026
The risk has deteriorated. El Niño weather patterns have begun to affect the Dry Corridor region in Central America, driving up temperatures and reducing rainfall by up to 50% compared to typical levels for the season that normally begins in June. In Guatemala, Alta Verapaz and Western Highlands regions have experienced irregular rainfall and elevated temperatures since June, resulting in reduced harvests and a decline in agricultural labour opportunities, which in turn have reduced household income for families dependent on seasonal agricultural employment. As a result, the number of people in need of food assistance in Guatemala is projected to reach up to 2.49 million by August. A similar impact is expected in Honduras, particularly in Choluteca region and along the Dry Corridor, where El Niño impacts have reduced agricultural production and labour demand, exposing 750,000 people to food insecurity by August. Erratic, below-average rainfall and high temperatures brought by El Niño have also affected the western and Dry Corridor areas of El Salvador, depleting food reserves among smallholder farmers and agricultural workers and diminishing their food purchasing capacity. That said, the number of people expected to face food insecurity needs in El Salvador is not projected to reach the same scale as in Guatemala. Compounding these impacts, food prices have risen across most of the Dry Corridor in all three countries, driven by a combination of reduced food supply, increased demand as agricultural households are forced to purchase food they would otherwise produce, and price increases linked to rising inflation. ([FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/es/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala/perspectiva-de-seguridad-alimentaria/junio-2026/print); [Fews Net 31/06/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/el-salvador/key-message-update/may-2026/print), [FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/honduras/food-security-outlook/june-2026/print), [NOA 11/07/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))


UPDATE 03/07/2026
The risk has deteriorated as El Niño weather patterns have begun to produce measurable humanitarian impacts across the Dry Corridor. In Guatemala, irregular rainfall has caused crops to dry out before harvest, forcing Indigenous communities to draw on food reserves or financial resources to meet their nutritional needs. In El Salvador, authorities have confirmed that the entire country, including Dry Corridor provinces, is already under El Niño influence, with below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures forecast for July 2026. The most recent manifestation was a 12-day heat wave that sustained abnormally elevated temperatures across the country. In Honduras, El Niño-associated drought, compounded by dependence on staple crops such as maize and beans, has already reduced both planting areas and harvest yields during the primary mid-year agricultural season.
These developments are unfolding across a region that is home to ten million people, of whom approximately 80% depend directly on agricultural production for their livelihoods. As El Niño conditions persist and drought intensifies, declining food production is expected to place severe pressure on subsistence farming households in the Dry Corridor and all others across the three countries who rely on the market purchase of staple crops to meet their daily food needs. ([Canal 26 YouTube 05/06/2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yzz6fBOKmU0), [SWI 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/gobierno-de-el-salvador-confirma-influencia-de-el-ni%C3%B1o%2C-con-m%C3%A1s-calor-y-menos-lluvias/91707068), [Infobae 30/06/2026](https://www.infobae.com/el-salvador/2026/06/30/corredor-seco-en-alerta-sequias-por-el-nino-violencia-y-un-recorte-del-59-de-la-ayuda-empujan-a-guatemala-y-honduras-al-limite/), [NOAA 11/06/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))

R1072.title: Escalating civil unrest leads to increased protection risks and poverty
R1072.what_happened: The impact of the post-election unrest has been severe and widespread, with significant humanitarian, political, and economic consequences. By March 2025, over 350 people had been killed, thousands injured – including gunshot victims – and nearly 4,0...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The hazard of post-election civil unrest and political instability in Mozambique has materialised following the highly contested general elections held on 9 October 2024. Allegations of electoral fraud, vote tampering, and the exclusion of opposition voices quickly led to widespread protests after opposition candidate Venâncio Mondlane rejected the official results. Since 21 October, the country has experienced sustained demonstrations, general strikes, and riots, erupting across major urban centres including Maputo, Nampula, and Zambezia. These events confirm the realisation of the anticipated hazard, as tensions escalated owing to the Government's refusal to acknowledge opposition claims and the increasing polarisation of the political environment. The unrest has intensified with the killing of opposition figures, the use of live ammunition by the police, and growing public anger, evolving from election-related protests into broader anti-government movements.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The impact of the post-election unrest has been severe and widespread, with significant humanitarian, political, and economic consequences. By March 2025, over 350 people had been killed, thousands injured  – including gunshot victims – and nearly 4,000 arrested or detained, including children. There have also been documented cases of forced disappearances and unlawful detentions, further aggravating public outrage and eroding trust in state institutions. The unrest has led to large-scale disruptions, including the temporary closure of the South African border, a shutdown of Maputo port operations for over a month, electricity supply restrictions, and the paralysis of key urban infrastructure. The national economy contracted by 4.87% in the last quarter of 2024, highlighting the severe economic toll. Public grievances have expanded beyond the election results to include corruption, poverty, and the rising cost of living, as evidenced by the vandalism of Frelimo headquarters in February 2025.

UPDATE 24/11/2025
This risk has largely materialised. Until 24 November 2025, about 187,000 people remained displaced owing to clashes and insecurity in Al Sweida governorate. Since the clashes broke out between Druze and Bedouin communities in July, government forces have been struggling to restore safety and security, indicating their weak control over armed groups. The people affected continue to face disruptions in services, such as shortages in health supplies, intermittent constraints in access, and deteriorating electricity and telecommunications services. High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, movement restrictions, and sporadic security incidents, including explosive ordnance-related casualties. Needs for food continue to be high, driven by shortages of bread given the limited supplies entering the governorate, resulting in the closure of bakeries. Humanitarian aid trucks can enter the governorate, but tensions and sporadic violence along key routes, such as the Damascus–Al Sweida route, often restrict access. These also limit civilian movement and access to essential services. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))


UPDATE 23/07/2025
Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. 
As of 21 July, the clashes displaced at least 93,000 people, mostly within Al Sweida, others went to Dar’a and Rural Damascus governorates. IDPs are staying with relatives or public building such as schools and mosques, and they need shelter, ready to eat meals, clean water, and medical care. Power outages, unstable internet and mobile connection, and severe shortage in water supply and medical services are reported in Al Sweida. ([UNHCR 21/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/fba9ec77-7b57-4aa0-849e-4a43472838a4/EXTERNAL%20%233%20Flash%20update%20on%20the%20situation%20in%20Sweida%2021%20July%202025.pdf), [SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))
