Fodder shortages are increasingly affecting pastoral households. At the same time, the return of over 2 million Afghans from Iran and Pakistan continues to strain food systems and water resources, particularly in border provinces. ([FEWS Net 04/2026](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/seasonal-monitor/april-2026), [FAO 06/04/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/f46a1cd6-f0d8-4440-8829-2d0f4d051bfe/content), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025))
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 31/03/2026
As of March 2026, Afghanistan faces escalating climate-driven risks linked to ongoing La Niña conditions that began in October 2025. Below-average snowfall and rainfall, combined with above-normal temperatures, are reinforcing drought conditions nationwide. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions are particularly affected, with rising agricultural and hydrological drought risks. This follows four consecutive years (2022–2025) of below-average production and crop failures in key regions. Second-season crops in 2025, including rice, maize, and cotton, have been impacted, while reduced winter precipitation threatens 2026 wheat production. Limited snowmelt and weakened river flows are expected to worsen water scarcity, constraining irrigation, pasture growth, and drinking water access. Pastoralist households face fodder shortages, reducing livestock productivity. Combined with earthquake impacts and large-scale population movements, these overlapping shocks are intensifying food insecurity, straining livelihoods, and overwhelming coping capacities ahead of the 2026 lean season. ([Fews Net 04/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-favorable-soil-moisture-conditions-are-beneficial-spring-wheat-planting-march-3-2026), [AP News 30/03/2026](https://apnews.com/article/weather-floods-afghanistan-storm-landslide-e6be89ef89f32f5d8c68f3380bdebbe7), [FAO 21/01/2026](https://media.un.org/unifeed/en/asset/d352/d3526668), [Reuters 03/03/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/un-warns-200000-more-afghan-children-face-acute-malnutrition-2026-2026-03-03/)    


UPDATE 09/02/2026
In February 2026, drought risk remains high across the country. Despite some improvements in western areas, multiple sources confirm the persistence of below-average winter precipitation, low snowpack, and above-average temperatures, continuing to place significant strain on water availability, agricultural production, and food systems. The 2025 wet season began significantly below average from October–November across most areas, leading to widespread deficits. Late rains, combined with low soil moisture from earlier months, disrupted rain-fed winter wheat planting, particularly in the north and northeast, and reduced the overall planted area. Between October 2025 and January 2026, southern provinces, especially Helmand and Kandahar, experienced the highest precipitation deficits of 30–60% below average. This is constraining irrigation supplies and increasing soil moisture stress ahead of the spring 2026 agricultural season.
The WFP estimates that 17.4 million people will face acute food insecurity through March 2026, including nearly five million malnourished women and children. These outcomes are driven in part by drought-related impacts on crops and rural livelihoods, compounded by economic shocks and large-scale returnee inflows. ([FEWS NET 02/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-january-precipitation-reduced-seasonal-deficits-benefiting-surface-and-groundwater-resources-february-2-2026), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025#:~:text=Some%20seasonal%20improvement%20is%20expected,levels%20of%20acute%20food%20insecurity.), [Crop Monitor 05/02/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [WFP accessed 09/02/2025](https://www.wfp.org/countries/afghanistan), [FAO 06/01/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/46600ceb-a104-4223-88e9-0ccfae273327/content))

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed the pipeline that carries oil to Khartoum. The pipeline was reopened after two days, following a meeting with government officials. In response, Arab tribes in Kassala state protested against the Beja tribes’ blocking of roads and ports. The Beja tribes continued to block Red Sea ports and highways connecting eastern Sudan with the rest of the country until mid-October 2021. The Government warned that the country was running out of life-saving medicines, fuel, and wheat stocks.

R1037.title: Establishment of military regime leads to increased conflict and spread of violence across Sudan
R1037.what_happened: After the removal of Omar Al Bashir in April 2019, Sudan's Transitional Military Council (TMC) faced massive protests led by the Forces of Freedom and Change. Protesters demanded a transition to civilian rule, accusing the TMC of perpetuating Al Bash...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: After the removal of Omar Al Bashir in April 2019, Sudan's Transitional Military Council (TMC) faced massive protests led by the Forces of Freedom and Change. Protesters demanded a transition to civilian rule, accusing the TMC of perpetuating Al Bashir's authoritarian regime. Tensions escalated on 3 June when the Rapid Support Forces violently dispersed a peaceful sit-in in Khartoum, killing over 100 people. Persistent demonstrations and mediation efforts resulted in a power-sharing agreement in August that established a joint military-civilian Sovereign Council to lead the transition.

evolution.hazard_materialisation: In response to the escalating activities of armed groups, including the March 23 Movement (M23), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) dispatched the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF) in November 2022. This multinational force, comprising troops from Kenya, Burundi, South Sudan, and Uganda, was deployed to bring stability to the conflict-torn eastern regions of the DRC. However, the presence of the EACRF led to heightened clashes between military forces and various armed factions, exacerbating security challenges in the region. These clashes caused a large number of civilians to leave conflict zones, increasing the need for humanitarian aid in the region. The departure of the EACRF in December 2023 created a security gap that was swiftly taken advantage of by armed groups, further exacerbating instability.
evolution.impact_materialisation: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian crisis, with critical needs in areas such as shelter, food, water, sanitation, and medical care. The situation has been aggravated by the suspension of activities by numerous humanitarian organisations due to persistent insecurity.

evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 24/11/2025
This risk has largely materialised. Until 24 November 2025, about 187,000 people remained displaced owing to clashes and insecurity in Al Sweida governorate. Since the clashes broke out between Druze and Bedouin communities in July, government forces have been struggling to restore safety and security, indicating their weak control over armed groups. The people affected continue to face disruptions in services, such as shortages in health supplies, intermittent constraints in access, and deteriorating electricity and telecommunications services. High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, movement restrictions, and sporadic security incidents, including explosive ordnance-related casualties. Needs for food continue to be high, driven by shortages of bread given the limited supplies entering the governorate, resulting in the closure of bakeries. Humanitarian aid trucks can enter the governorate, but tensions and sporadic violence along key routes, such as the Damascus–Al Sweida route, often restrict access. These also limit civilian movement and access to essential services. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))


UPDATE 23/07/2025
Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. 
As of 21 July, the clashes displaced at least 93,000 people, mostly within Al Sweida, others went to Dar’a and Rural Damascus governorates. IDPs are staying with relatives or public building such as schools and mosques, and they need shelter, ready to eat meals, clean water, and medical care. Power outages, unstable internet and mobile connection, and severe shortage in water supply and medical services are reported in Al Sweida. ([UNHCR 21/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/fba9ec77-7b57-4aa0-849e-4a43472838a4/EXTERNAL%20%233%20Flash%20update%20on%20the%20situation%20in%20Sweida%2021%20July%202025.pdf), [SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The economic crisis in Sudan, which began in 2018, continued to worsen in the following years due to the government's inability to address the underlying challenges holistically.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The country faced severe shortages of hard currency and basic commodities like fuel, flour, and medicines, leading to skyrocketing prices. Households across Sudan, including most IDPs, struggled to meet their basic needs as staple food prices for wheat, millet and sorghum increased by 150-200% in 2018. Limited access to food, reduced purchasing power, and few livelihood alternatives for farmers left an estimated 5.76 million people facing severe levels of food insecurity, especially in Khartoum, Red Sea, Blue Nile, White Nile, South Kordofan, Kassala, Gedaref and Darfur states.

R1051.title: Prolonged fuel shortages in Bangladesh worsen food security and disrupt health, telecommunications, and other essential services
R1051.what_happened: During August, gas and electricity shortages disrupted industrial production, transport, and household electricity access in Bangladesh. A temporary improvement in LNG supplies reduced load-shedding, but gas shortages continued to constrain industria...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The hazard materialised in August 2026 as persistent gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shortages translated into severe power supply disruptions and reduced industrial activity. On 3 August, average power generation shortfalls reached 1,482MW, with shortages reported across 62 of 143 generating units. Shortages were particularly acute in Dhaka, Khulna, Mymensingh, Rajshahi, and Rangpur divisions. By 18 August, power plants were receiving only 37.4% of their gas requirement, leaving 13 of 25 affected units unable to generate electricity. On 19 August, the Excelerate LNG terminal at Moheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, ran out of LNG, reducing national gas supply to 2,185mmcfd against demand of around 3,800mmcfd. ([The Daily Star 03/08/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/gas-shortage-sparks-extensive-power-cuts-4238811), [BD News24 18/08/2026](https://bdnews24.com/bangladesh/3746b783d5b0), [The Business Standard 19/08/2026](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/excelerate-fsru-halts-supply-again-four-days-after-resumption-1519786))
evolution.impact_materialisation: During August, gas and electricity shortages disrupted industrial production, transport, and household electricity access in Bangladesh. A temporary improvement in LNG supplies reduced load-shedding, but gas shortages continued to constrain industrial activity. Higher operating and transport costs, poultry losses, and rising food prices further reduced household purchasing power, while factory closures threatened workers’ incomes. Agricultural production also came under increasing pressure. Despite adequate national fertiliser stocks, localised shortages, distribution constraints, and prices above official rates limited farmers’ access to inputs and could affect upcoming harvests. An estimated five million people are in need of agricultural assistance between June–November 2026, indicating a further deterioration in livelihoods and food availability. ([FAO 27/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/bangladesh/bangladesh-diem-monitoring-emergency-agriculture-support-brief-july-2026-round-14), [Dhaka Tribune 26/08/2026](https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/agriculture/418350/fertilizer-crisis-what-is-driving-shortages-and), [The Daily Star 19/08/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/power-and-energy/news/moheshkhali-terminal-runs-out-lng-bangladeshs-gas-supply-falls-below-2200-mmcfd-4251721), [The Business Standard 24/08/2026](https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/gas-power-crisis-ripples-food-transport-construction-1523111), [The Daily Star 18/08/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/gas-supply-improves-industries-still-struggle-4250406), [Prothom Alo 11/08/2026](https://en.prothomalo.com/bangladesh/sa0o4n1lhk))
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 12/07/2026
The Haor region was hit by flash floods from pre-monsoon rainfall and upstream inflows during peak Boro harvest, damaging cropland in districts reliant on a single annual crop cycle. Farmers are facing crop losses, debt, and forced sales of wet paddy at reduced prices. Boro output is estimated to be down to 10% nationally. QatarEnergy, Bangladesh's largest LNG supplier, halved its 2026 scheduled deliveries, with Petrobangla citing Hormuz-related war disruptions and turning to costlier spot market purchases. 15.3 million people are estimated to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food insecurity in May–August, rising to 18.1 million by September–December. ([Reuters 06/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/qatarenergy-halves-2026-scheduled-deliveries-lng-bangladesh-says-petrobangla-2026-07-06/), [IPC 30/06/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Bangladesh_Acute_Food_Insecurity_May_Dec2026_Report.pdf), [The Daily Star 01/05/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/business/economy/news/what-it-means-rice-production-and-prices-4165046))


UPDATE 14/06/2026
Available indicators suggest that the crisis has continued to deteriorate. The Government implemented two fuel price hikes, the first in April and again on 1 June, with diesel now at 115 Bangladeshi taka (USD 0.93) and petrol at 140 Bangladeshi taka (USD 1.14) per litre. Electricity tariffs were raised by 16.7%, compounding household expenditure pressures. Inflation reached a 16-month high of 9.42% in May 2026, driven by food (9.06%), housing (9.26%), and transport (9.86%), further eroding the purchasing power of low-income households. Hormuz disruptions now also threaten fertiliser supply chains, with 30–35% of global fertiliser trade transiting the route, raising acute concerns for crop yield impacts beyond the Boro season into the upcoming Aman season (rice cultivation seasons).
([The Daily Start 31/05/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/environment/natural-resources/energy/news/fuel-prices-rise-again-petrol-octane-tk-5-litre-4187466),[TBS 04/06/2026]( https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/retail-power-tariff-hiked-tk152-amid-subsidy-cuts-1453181), [Trading Economics accessed 14/06/2026]( https://tradingeconomics.com/bangladesh/inflation-cpi))

R1052.title: Tensions between the military and political components in Sudan’s transitional government result in social unrest and increased access constraints for humanitarian organisations
R1052.what_happened: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed th...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed the pipeline that carries oil to Khartoum. The pipeline was reopened after two days, following a meeting with government officials. In response, Arab tribes in Kassala state protested against the Beja tribes’ blocking of roads and ports. The Beja tribes continued to block Red Sea ports and highways connecting eastern Sudan with the rest of the country until mid-October 2021. The Government warned that the country was running out of life-saving medicines, fuel, and wheat stocks.

R1052.title: Failure of essential services owing to the blockade in Mali leads to civil unrest and destabilisation and aggravates needs
R1052.what_happened: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several region...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: JNIM's blockade strategy expanded beyond northern and central Mali into southern and western regions, targeting fuel convoys, transport corridors, and economic infrastructure. The blockade persisted throughout the monitoring period despite temporary fluctuations in fuel availability and continued to disrupt national supply chains and state control over key transport routes.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several regions. While large-scale civil unrest did not materialise, the blockade contributed to worsening humanitarian conditions, weakened state authority, and increased insecurity. Ongoing blockade-related dynamics are now captured under the new Mali risk on coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 27/04/2026
The risk remains high and increasingly volatile. While there were indications of a partial easing in the intensity of the fuel blockade earlier in April 2026, recent large-scale coordinated attacks across multiple cities highlight a renewed deterioration in the security environment. Attacks targeting key locations, including Kati near Bamako, and the reported death of the Minister of Defence underscore the extent of armed groups’ operational reach. These developments are likely to further undermine the State’s ability to secure key transport corridors and ensure the continuity of fuel supply, which remains heavily dependent on military-escorted convoys. The reported loss of control over areas such as Kidal and the withdrawal of allied forces also point to weakening state authority in strategic regions. As a result, the risk of renewed disruptions to fuel supply and essential services remains high. Combined with continued fuel price increases and inflationary pressures, this may further constrain access to electricity, healthcare, and markets, while increasing the likelihood of social tensions. Overall, recent events suggest that earlier improvements were fragile and that the structural drivers of the risk remain firmly in place. ([RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [RFI 02/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260402-mali-autorit%C3%A9s-accusent-des-entreprises-utiliser-crise-carburant-pour-gonfler-leurs-prix), [BBC 24/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/afrique/articles/cyv1rpn4753o), [Ledjely 01/04/2026](https://ledjely.com/2026/04/01/mali-la-hausse-du-carburant-fait-craindre-une-spirale-des-prix/), [Timbuktu Institute 17/04/2026](https://timbuktu-institute.org/index.php/toutes-l-actualites/item/1509-le-mali-entre-chocs-externes-et-defis-internes))


UPDATE 30/03/2026
The risk has slightly deteriorated, with more fuel shortages reported. On 28 March 2026, the Government of Mali raised diesel prices by nearly 30% and petrol prices by 13% in response to supply disruptions by the Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin blockade. The heightened impacts of the fuel shortages increase the likelihood of civil unrest. On 25 March, diesel shortages in Bamako intensified as limited fuel imports were further redirected to support electricity generation during a heat wave. Several fuel stations ran out of diesel, leading to long queues at remaining supply points and disrupting urban mobility. At least 100 public transport vehicles were taken out of service, while construction-related transport (e.g. sand and gravel trucks) halted. ([TRT 10/03/2026](https://www.trtafrika.com/article/27f0213a3997), [Bloomberg 28/03/2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-28/mali-raises-petrol-diesel-prices-and-cuts-some-fuel-subsidies))


UPDATE 26/02/2026
Since January, the risk linked to the fuel blockade and related insecurity has remained high and volatile, with continued attacks despite temporary supply improvements in Bamako. While fuel availability in the capital improved in early February, the broader trend points to sustained operational disruption and geographic expansion of insecurity.  Key developments include renewed large-scale JNIM attacks on fuel convoys near Kayes, leading to the killing of drivers and military escorts and prompting a nationwide transport strike on 9 February. In central Mali, state forces conducted airstrikes in Macina (Ségou Region) following reported insurgent activity in Sikasso, while in Kidal region, a convoy was targeted by both JNIM and Azawad Liberation Front elements, suggesting overlapping armed actor pressure in the north. Continued road blockades affecting multiple localities and persistent electricity shortages (6–8 hours per day in Bamako) indicate structural fragility. In the short to medium term, continued convoy insecurity and transport disruptions risk renewed fuel shortages, rising prices, reduced market access, and further constraints on electricity supply, livelihoods, and humanitarian access, particularly outside the capital. ([DW 10/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/fr/focus-sahel-plus-villes-sous-blocus-du-jnim-au-mali/a-75901357), [RFI 03/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260203-au-mali-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-plie-mais-ne-rompt-pas), [RFI 10/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260210-mali-cibles-d-attaques-jihadistes-des-chauffeurs-routiers-appellent-%C3%A0-un-arr%C3%AAt-de-travail), [RFI 20/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260220-mali-une-frappe-de-drone-des-rebelles-du-fla-contre-l-arm%C3%A9e-fait-des-morts-des-deux-c%C3%B4t%C3%A9s)). 


UPDATE 02/02/2026
Since the previous update, the risk associated with the fuel blockade has remained elevated but volatile, with short-lived improvements followed by renewed disruption. While some fuel circulation has resumed intermittently, shortages persisted throughout January 2026, indicating neither clear escalation nor stabilisation. Key developments point to a broadening of the blockade’s scope. In Bamako, electricity supply remains limited to around five to seven hours per day, and fuel availability continues to be intermittent, with long queues and growing reliance on informal markets. In the southwest, Nioro du Sahel remains under a near-total blockade since early September 2025, with movement restrictions, reported abductions, and the increasing scarcity of food, medicines, fuel, and water. In parallel, attacks linked to Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin have expanded beyond fuel convoys to economic infrastructure, including mid-January 2026 attacks on industrial sites in Kayes and late January attacks on fuel convoys. Authorities have announced tighter fuel controls and reinforced escorts ahead of Ramadan, but continued incidents suggest a persistent risk of disruption to essential services, rising living costs, constrained access to markets, and increasing humanitarian needs in affected urban and blockaded areas. ([RFI 10/01/2026)[https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260110-mali-des-habitants-de-nioro-du-sahel-racontent-le-blocus-jihadiste-qui-dure-depuis-cinq-mois), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-la-fourniture-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-de-carburant-reste-tr%C3%A8s-insuffisante-les-bamakois-se-r%C3%A9signent), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-le-manque-de-carburant-%C3%A0-l-a%C3%A9roport-de-bamako-perturbe-certaines-liaisons), [RFI 16/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260116-mali-blocus-jihadiste-%C3%A0-nioro-du-sahel-la-situation-est-sous-contr%C3%B4le-selon-les-autorit%C3%A9s-de-transition), [RFI 12/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260112-mali-comment-et-pourquoi-des-jihadistes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-trois-sites-industriels-de-la-r%C3%A9gion-de-kayes), [RFI 02/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260202-au-mali-les-autorit%C3%A9s-veulent-s%C3%A9curiser-l-apprivisionnement-de-carburant-pour-le-mois-de-ramadan))


UPDATE 18/12/2025
Since early December, the JNIM has resumed attacks on fuel convoys after a temporary slowdown observed in late November. The initial lull allowed some fuel deliveries to reach Bamako and Mopti, briefly reducing shortages and restoring limited electricity and public services. However, renewed ambushes in Bougouni, Ouélessébougou, and Ségou, including the destruction of over 15 fuel tankers and the killing of drivers, have reinstated supply chain disruptions and public anxiety. In Bamako, queues at petrol stations have grown again, diesel has become scarce, and intermittent power cuts have returned. While 300 trucks were received ahead of the AES summit in mid-December, the improvement remains temporary. In Mopti and surrounding areas, fuel convoys have resumed under heavy military protection, but the quantities remain insufficient to meet the demand. Electricity has returned for around nine hours per day, and some economic activity has restarted, though fuel prices on the black market remain triple the official rate.  The blockade continues to affect humanitarian operations and access to essential services. In areas such as Koulikoro, Sikasso, and Koutiala, fuel scarcity persists, with limited electricity, inaccessible health services, and rising transport costs. The JNIM’s strategy has evolved beyond physical control, aiming to delegitimise the state through economic strangulation and selective violence. The group is reportedly consolidating control over rural areas by offering basic services (such as justice and security) under Islamic governance, gradually normalising its authority.

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Protests by non-Arab tribes in eastern Sudan, which started in mid-September 2021, have intensified after the coup attempt as fears about the military taking over the Government increased. The Beja tribes shut down ports, blocked roads, and closed the pipeline that carries oil to Khartoum. The pipeline was reopened after two days, following a meeting with government officials. In response, Arab tribes in Kassala state protested against the Beja tribes’ blocking of roads and ports. The Beja tribes continued to block Red Sea ports and highways connecting eastern Sudan with the rest of the country until mid-October 2021. The Government warned that the country was running out of life-saving medicines, fuel, and wheat stocks.

evolution.hazard_materialisation: On 30 March 2026, federal forces backed by allied clan militias entered Baidoa following weeks of escalating political tensions, engaging in brief but heavy clashes with Southwest State regional forces before assuming control of the city. Southwest State President Laftagareen resigned and fled to Kenya. Further clashes between federal forces and Laftagareen loyalists erupted on the outskirts of Baidoa in late May 2026. Elections in Southwest State are currently underway amid continued instability. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))
evolution.impact_materialisation: The clashes and prolonged fear of wider confrontation triggered pre-emptive mass displacement of over 50,000 people, predominantly women and children, from Baidoa towards Burhakaba, Hudur, Waajid, and surrounding areas. Three people were killed and five injured. Schools, hospitals, and maternal and child health centres were temporarily closed. Displaced populations faced heightened protection risks including overcrowding, inadequate shelter, and gender-based violence exposure, compounding already severe drought-related displacement and food insecurity across Bay and Bakool. Some families have begun returning, though conditions remain fragile. Broader risks related to the federal–state constitutional tensions are captured under the Somalia constitutional crisis risk. ([UNHCR 01/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/flash-12-over-50000-people-displaced-following-political-escalation-baidoa-south-west-state), [Garowe Online 22/05/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-clashes-erupt-outside-baidoa-between-federal-troops-and-forces-loyal-to-ousted-southwest-leader), [Hiiraan 27/05/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/security4/2026/May/205279/heavy_fighting_erupts_near_baidoa_between_federal_forces_and_laftagareen_loyalists.aspx))

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Clashes between Hezbollah and Israel continued to escalate, especially in September 2024. On 23 September, the Israeli army increased their military attacks, with over 330 raids targeting over 117 towns and cities in southern Lebanon (South and Nabatiye governorates), Bekaa governorate, and the southern suburbs of Beirut city in Beirut governorate. A ceasefire agreement was reached in November 2024, calling for a 60-day time frame for Hezbollah fighters and Israeli forces to withdraw from areas south of the Litani River, but reports indicate that Israel has continued military activities in southern Lebanon.
evolution.impact_materialisation: Before the ceasefire agreement was reached in November, the conflict had displaced nearly 900,000 people in Lebanon, with many seeking refuge in temporary shelters or with host families. Southern Lebanon's agricultural sector has been severely affected, with over 1,240 hectares of land damaged and approximately 340,000 farm animals lost. The use of white phosphorus bombs has rendered many farmlands unfit for cultivation, affecting food security levels in Lebanon. The Lebanese economy is projected to contract by 12.81% by January 2025, with agriculture, manufacturing, and services in South governorate and Bekaa Valley being particularly hard-hit.

R1055.title: Intensifying humanitarian and security crisis in Kenya worsens conditions in refugee camps
R1055.what_happened: The situation in Kenya’s refugee-hosting areas has escalated into a full-scale humanitarian crisis, marking clear impact materialisation. Food ration cuts and funding shortages have left 85,000 refugees nearly half the camp populations in Kakuma and...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Kenya’s humanitarian and security situation deteriorates, particularly in refugee-hosting areas such as Garissa and Turkana counties. This systemic breakdown in assistance created a volatile environment, heightening tensions between refugees and host communities, and sparking protests and violent clashes, such as those in Kalobeyei in late June 2025. At the same time, rising insecurity, resource scarcity, and disease outbreaks including dengue fever in Dadaab have compounded the fragility of the camps.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The situation in Kenya’s refugee-hosting areas has escalated into a full-scale humanitarian crisis, marking clear impact materialisation. Food ration cuts and funding shortages have left 85,000 refugees nearly half the camp populations in Kakuma and Kalobeyei without assistance, triggering widespread hunger, protests, and violent clashes with police. As conditions deteriorated, more than 9,300 South Sudanese refugees have returned home since June 2025, many through Nadapal into Eastern Equatoria. The majority are children, now exposed to ambushes, unsafe border conditions, poor sanitation, and heightened risks of gender-based violence (GBV) and disease. Within the camps, worsening socioeconomic conditions have driven a spike in crime, GBV, and early or forced marriages, while malnutrition among children and pregnant or lactating women continues to rise. Water shortages, service interruptions, and dengue fever outbreaks in Dadaab further reflect the strain on essential services. Host communities are increasingly overstretched, facing overcrowding, food insecurity, and limited access to health and shelter, amplifying humanitarian needs for both refugees and hosts.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 10/09/2025
Since June 2025, over 9,300 South Sudanese refugees have returned from Kakuma and Kalobeyei camps in Kenya, with daily arrivals peaking at over 220 in August. The movement is prompted by food ration cuts that have left 85,000 (45% of camp populations) without assistance, triggering protests. Kakuma and Kalobeyei were hosting nearly 191,000 South Sudanese refugees prior to the new arrivals. Two-thirds of the returnees are children, many arriving through Nadapal town into eastern Equatoria before moving to Budi, Ikotos, Kapoeta, and Torit towns. Families face ambush risks, lack of reception facilities, unsafe sanitation, and exposure to gender-based violence and disease at the border. While many returnees rejoin relatives, host households are increasingly overstretched, leading to overcrowding, food insecurity, and limited health and shelter access. Urgent needs include food, safe water, health services, and protection support especially for children and women, alongside assistance for host communities. ([UNHCR 11/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/south-sudan/emergency-update-returns-kenya-south-sudan), [TRT Afrika 29/08/2025](https://www.trtafrika.com/english/article/7d3492517a31), [Radio Tamazuj 14/08/2025](https://www.radiotamazuj.org/en/news/article/over-350-refugees-arrive-torit-following-food-cuts-in-kenyan-camp#:~:text=Over%20350%20refugees%20arrive%20Torit,in%20Kenyan%20camp%20%2D%20Radio%20Tamazuj))

UPDATE 05/07/2025
Worsening socioeconomic conditions heightened by funding shortfalls are fuelling a rise in crime, heightening tensions between refugee and host communities, and triggering renewed protests over limited access to essential services. On 28 June 2025, a protest in Kalobeyei settlement turned violent following clashes between refugees and police. Across all camps, malnutrition is increasing, especially among children, pregnant or lactating women, and individuals with chronic illnesses, as a result of severe reductions in food rations. Gender-based violence, including intimate partner violence and early or forced marriage, remains widespread as a result of economic hardship, entrenched social norms, and overcrowded living conditions. In Kakuma and Kalobeyei, water shortages and service interruptions have led to internal relocations, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations. Access to protection, shelter, and education remains inadequate, with girls at heightened risk of early marriage and boys pushed into informal labour. At the same time, dengue fever outbreaks in Ifo and Dagahaley camps in Dadaab have been linked to poor waste management, rising temperatures, and constrained healthcare access. ([ECHO 29/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/kenya/kenya-humanitarian-situation-refugee-camps-dg-echo-drc-echo-daily-flash-29-july-2025), [Radio Ergo 22/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/kenya/job-losses-and-aid-cuts-leave-dadaab-refugees-uncertain-their-future))

R1055.title: The deployment of the regional military force leads to more displacement and increased humanitarian needs in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
R1055.what_happened: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian cri...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: In response to the escalating activities of armed groups, including the March 23 Movement (M23), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) dispatched the East African Community Regional Force (EACRF) in November 2022. This multinational force, comprising troops from Kenya, Burundi, South Sudan, and Uganda, was deployed to bring stability to the conflict-torn eastern regions of the DRC. However, the presence of the EACRF led to heightened clashes between military forces and various armed factions, exacerbating security challenges in the region. These clashes caused a large number of civilians to leave conflict zones, increasing the need for humanitarian aid in the region. The departure of the EACRF in December 2023 created a security gap that was swiftly taken advantage of by armed groups, further exacerbating instability.
evolution.impact_materialisation: Since January 2025, about 450,000 people have been displaced due to renewed violence, especially after the M23 captured key cities, such as Goma and Bukavu. These military operations and the resulting instability have exacerbated the humanitarian crisis, with critical needs in areas such as shelter, food, water, sanitation, and medical care. The situation has been aggravated by the suspension of activities by numerous humanitarian organisations due to persistent insecurity.

R1068.title: Further Israeli expansion in southern Syria triggers armed group resistance, displacement, and heightened food insecurity
R1068.what_happened: The expected humanitarian impacts partially materialised. Continued Israeli incursions displaced additional households, damaged homes, roads, water infrastructure, and agricultural land, and restricted civilian access to farmland and essential servic...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: The hazard partially materialised. Israel continued to expand and consolidate its military presence in southern Syria through repeated ground incursions, arrests, checkpoints, civilian property destruction, and movement restrictions, particularly across Quneitra and western Dar’a governorates. Israeli forces established additional military positions and normalised near-daily operations inside Syrian territory, while protests against the continued military presence increased from June–July 2026, reflecting growing civilian resentment. Israel also continued to justify its operations on security grounds and the protection of Druze communities. That said, the risk overestimated the likelihood that Israeli expansion would trigger sustained armed resistance by Syrian factions or Iran-backed groups. Instead, opposition remained largely limited to local protests and isolated confrontations, while the transitional Government continued to avoid direct military confrontation with Israel. Likewise, Israeli operations did not expand into the broader territorial advance towards As Sweida or the Damascus–As Sweida highway suggested in the risk.
evolution.impact_materialisation:
The expected humanitarian impacts partially materialised. Continued Israeli incursions displaced additional households, damaged homes, roads, water infrastructure, and agricultural land, and restricted civilian access to farmland and essential services in affected communities, increasing humanitarian needs and disrupting livelihoods.

Displacement directly attributable to Israeli military operations in southern Syria remained fragmented and underreported. The most documented case of permanent displacement occurred in Al Hamidiyah, Quneitra, where Israel forcibly expelled 12 families by demolishing 16 homes to construct a military base in the months after December 2024. Incident-specific figures point to larger but temporary movements; an Israeli incursion in Beit Jinn, Rural Damascus, in November 2025 temporarily displaced approximately 1,500 people, while the Israeli shelling of Abdin village in western Dar’a on 29 June 2026 caused around 2,000 residents to flee to neighbouring villages, most of whom returned shortly after.

Humanitarian responders also reported growing protection concerns linked to arrests, movement restrictions, and repeated military operations in Quneitra and Dar’a. That said, the anticipated scale of displacement did not materialise. There was no evidence of a large-scale offensive comparable to the 2018 Dar’a campaign or significant cross-border displacement into Jordan.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 09/07/2026
The risk has further deteriorated as Israeli military expansion in southern Syria continues to drive local tensions, with protests against Israel’s advances and continued presence in Syrian territory reported in southern governorates in June 2026. The demonstrations in As Sweida and surrounding areas reflected the growing opposition of communities to Israeli military activity and concerns over sovereignty, despite Israel’s stated objective of preventing threats from armed groups and protecting Druze communities. The protests indicate that Israeli expansion risks increasing local resentment and could contribute to further instability, particularly in Druze-majority areas, where Israel has sought to position itself as a security party. ([SANA 19/06/2026](https://sana.sy/en/photos/2324228/), [Arab News 30/06/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649041/middle-east), [AJ 29/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/29/new-israeli-assault-in-southern-syria-forces-families-to-flee-their-homes))


UPDATE 27/04/2026
The risk has deteriorated. Israeli incursions in April 2026 reflected a pattern of near-daily raids, arrests, and movement restrictions in southern Syria. On 11 April, Israeli forces conducted incursions into the towns of Kudna in Quneitra governorate and Wadi Al Raqad and Hamata in Daraa, by the Yarmouk Basin, arresting at least three civilians during house raids. The operations followed artillery shelling on 10 April targeting Jamlah town, damaging agricultural land. Around 12 military vehicles were involved in at least one incursion. Later in the month, protests erupted in southern Syria and Damascus, organised by families of Syrians detained by Israeli forces, indicating a deterioration in the risk given the increase in Israeli raids. ([AJ 11/04/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/4/11/%D9%82%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%BA%D9%84-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B9%D8%A7), [EB 27/04/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/04/damascus-protesters-urge-action-on-syrians-held-by-israel/))

UPDATE 30/03/2026
The risk continues to be valid but stable. On 28 March 2026, Israeli forces arrested a Syrian man and a child in southern Quneitra and conducted a ground incursion into Jbata Al Khashab town in the north, including house raids and searches. These incidents are part of a pattern of near-daily incursions in southern Syria involving the arrest of civilians, including herders and children. The continuation of these operations indicates a normalisation of Israeli ground activity inside Syrian territory, contributing to persistent insecurity in border communities. Recurrent raids, checkpoints, and arrests are likely to increase protection risks, restrict civilian movement and livelihoods, and further constrain the Syrian Government’s capacity to restore security, attract investment, and improve economic conditions in the south. ([AJ 01/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/3/1/%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B4%D8%AF-100-%D8%A3%D9%84%D9%81-%D9%85%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%B7-%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%86))

UPDATE 11/02/2026
Tensions in southern Syria have intensified since December 2025, driven by the Government's strategic shift towards consolidating control following its northeast offensive and Israel's continued military incursions.
A US-brokered agreement in January 2026 established joint Israeli–Syrian intelligence-sharing mechanisms on movements of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant, but negotiations stalled over future control of Mount Hermon, held by Israel since 2024. Israeli forces continued arrests and roadblocks in Quneitra governorate and launched strikes on Hezbollah targets on the Lebanese border post-agreement, demonstrating parallel diplomatic and military strategies. As Sweida Governor Mustafa Al Bakkour launched a ‘comprehensive settlement initiative’ to bring the governorate under state control, but Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, a prominent Druze spiritual leader, rejected this outright, demanding an independent Druze region with Israel as security guarantor. The Government has responded by providing services to undermine separatist narratives while strengthening its security posture. The collapse of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) represents a setback to Israel's reported strategy of fragmenting Syria into smaller constituent regions, potentially increasing Israeli reliance on Druze militias.
Key escalation risks are apparent. The Government's offensive against the SDF in the northeast may embolden further pursuit of a unitary Syrian state. Syrian forces recognise that Israeli intervention on behalf of Druze communities is highly probable, unlike US restraint during the SDF offensive. While the likeliest scenario is the current status quo, any southern escalation raises the potential for a protracted, multiparty conflict with substantially higher civilian displacement, humanitarian needs, and potential for prolonged instability compared to the rapid northeast campaign. Despite its relatively swift conclusion, the northeast offensive displaced 190,000 people at peak displacement; a protracted southern campaign could have deeper ramifications for large populations, including in the governorates of Dar'a (1.3 million), As Sweida (480,000 people), Quneitra (111,000), sections of Hama, and southern Rural Damascus.
([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [The National 07/02/2026](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/02/08/syrias-fragile-unity-faces-a-new-test-in-sweidas-druze-heartland/), [EUAA 02/12/2026](https://www.euaa.europa.eu/publications/country-guidance-syria-3), [The Syrian Observer 15/01/2026](https://syrianobserver.com/foreign-actors/israel-syria-security-agreement-stalls-over-mount-hermon-and-russian-presence.html), [IOM 31/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-emergency-mobility-tracking-situation-report-alepponorth-east-syria-nes-conflict-round-8-29-january-2026))

UPDATE 24/11/2025
In November, Israeli forces continued their incursions in southern Syria, specifically in the northern Quneitra governorate countryside. The Israeli army has advanced in civilian farmlands, destroyed hundreds of acres of forests, and uprooted olive trees, further disrupting people’s livelihoods. They have also arrested residents and established military checkpoints. In October, Israeli forces established a barrier preventing farmers from reaching their land and restricting civilian movement. For example, checkpoints and barriers set up by the Israeli army have cut off all communication between Hamidiyeh, one of the largest farming towns in the region, and Khan Arnaba, the economic and administrative centre of Quneitra. This has forcibly displaced dozens of families in Hamidiyeh from their homes, while those who remain depend highly on humanitarian aid. That said, aid is not always available because of humanitarian access restrictions, mainly road closures. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [HRW 17/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-israel-forcibly-displaces-villagers-occupied-south-enarhe), [Daily Sabah 22/11/2025](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/israel-expands-military-raids-into-syrias-southern-countryside), [Le Monde 10/11/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2025/11/10/on-the-syrian-golan-heights-israel-uses-the-same-tools-of-repression-as-in-the-west-bank_6747318_4.html))

UPDATE 23/07/2025
Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. Under the stated objective of protecting the Druze community, Israel carried out targeted airstrikes against Syrian military positions in Sweida and Damascus, including strategic sites like the Defence Ministry and areas near the presidential palace. These interventions, combined with Israel's reported coordination with the US to permit the deployment of Syrian Internal Security Forces, demonstrate its growing influence over the security dynamics in southern Syria. 
A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. ([SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 24/11/2025
This risk has largely materialised. Until 24 November 2025, about 187,000 people remained displaced owing to clashes and insecurity in Al Sweida governorate. Since the clashes broke out between Druze and Bedouin communities in July, government forces have been struggling to restore safety and security, indicating their weak control over armed groups. The people affected continue to face disruptions in services, such as shortages in health supplies, intermittent constraints in access, and deteriorating electricity and telecommunications services. High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, movement restrictions, and sporadic security incidents, including explosive ordnance-related casualties. Needs for food continue to be high, driven by shortages of bread given the limited supplies entering the governorate, resulting in the closure of bakeries. Humanitarian aid trucks can enter the governorate, but tensions and sporadic violence along key routes, such as the Damascus–Al Sweida route, often restrict access. These also limit civilian movement and access to essential services. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))


UPDATE 23/07/2025
Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. 
As of 21 July, the clashes displaced at least 93,000 people, mostly within Al Sweida, others went to Dar’a and Rural Damascus governorates. IDPs are staying with relatives or public building such as schools and mosques, and they need shelter, ready to eat meals, clean water, and medical care. Power outages, unstable internet and mobile connection, and severe shortage in water supply and medical services are reported in Al Sweida. ([UNHCR 21/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/fba9ec77-7b57-4aa0-849e-4a43472838a4/EXTERNAL%20%233%20Flash%20update%20on%20the%20situation%20in%20Sweida%2021%20July%202025.pdf), [SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

R1065.title: A return to large‑scale conflict in Gaza stokes a further deterioration of food security and humanitarian conditions
R1065.what_happened: The humanitarian impacts anticipated in the risk materialised. The sharp reduction in aid led to severe food shortages, with flour prices tripling and bread production declining by 50% because of shortages of flour and fuel. Humanitarian operations w...

evolution.hazard_materialisation: Although the October 2025 ceasefire was not formally terminated by July 2026, the hazard largely materialised, as hostilities intensified and humanitarian access deteriorated. Following the closure of Gaza's crossings on 1 March 2026, aid deliveries fell by around 80%, while Israel expanded military operations, controlling around 60% of the Gaza Strip by early June and announcing plans to seize 70% of the territory. Widespread evacuation orders and continued access restrictions further disrupted humanitarian operations.
evolution.impact_materialisation: The humanitarian impacts anticipated in the risk materialised. The sharp reduction in aid led to severe food shortages, with flour prices tripling and bread production declining by 50% because of shortages of flour and fuel. Humanitarian operations were disrupted, including World Central Kitchen reducing meal distributions by 50%. Malnutrition admissions increased by 21% between January–April compared with the same period in 2025, while food insecurity worsened as prolonged access restrictions and declining food availability further eroded households' already-depleted coping capacities.
evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 10/06/2026
Risk levels have increased as Netanyahu publicly announced on 28 May that he directed the IDF to take control of 70% of the Gaza Strip, far beyond the roughly 53% allotted under the October 2025 ceasefire deal with Hamas. At the beginning of June, Israel already controlled 60% of the Strip. Renewed Israeli military escalation in Gaza has led to rising civilian casualties and widespread displacement, with evacuation and shelter-in-place orders issued in multiple areas, including Gaza City, Deir Al Balah, Maghazi, Bureij, and Nuseirat. Between January–April 2026, malnutrition admissions increased by 21% compared to the same period in 2025 despite the ceasefire, indicating worsening food insecurity. By mid-May, World Central Kitchen, previously distributing around 1 million meals daily, reduced operations by 50% because of rising operational costs linked to the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruptions, affecting at least 13,000 displaced people across 12 camps in Khan Younis. ([WCK 14/05/2026](https://wck.org/news/wck-to-return-gaza-operations-to-pre-ceasefire-levels-amid-funding-challenges/), [Times of Israel 28/05/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-says-he-told-idf-to-seize-70-of-gaza-strip-well-beyond-terms-of-truce/), [UNRWA 26/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/unrwa-situation-report-223-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-west-bank-including-east-jerusalem-enar))


UPDATE 07/05/2026
The situation has deteriorated because Gaza faces further food access disruptions with the production of bread, a primary food source, dropping by 50% in late April given restricted aid deliveries, flour shortages, and a lack of fuel for running bakeries. Humanitarian access restrictions have increased since early March following the escalation in the Middle East involving Israeli and US attacks on Iran, resulting in decreased inflows into the Strip – currently at around 260 tonnes per day against a required 450 tonnes, equivalent to only 38% of pre-October 2023 levels. The bread bundles that international organisations can produce cover only 30% of needs. Food insecurity projections for mid-April suggest that 1.6 million may be facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels, likely worsening as restrictions on the entry of aid, including flour, persist. There are already reports of people queuing for hours for bread only to return without it. ([TNA 28/04/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/gazas-bread-crisis-deepens-50-production-cuts), [IPC 19/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/gaza-strip-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-and-acute-malnutrition-special-snapshot-october-2025-april-2026-published-19-december-2025), [WFP 23/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/wfp-palestine-emergency-response-external-situation-report-87-23-april-2026-reporting-period-1-14-april-2026))


UPDATE 26/03/2026
Although the conflict in the Middle East between Iran and Israel/US was not originally suggested as a trigger for this risk, it has contributed to a spike in food prices as most border crossings have been closed since 1 March 2026, except for Kerem Shalom for limited humanitarian movement and the Rafah border crossing for people’s movement only until 25 March. Aid deliveries into Gaza have dropped by around 80%, with only 590 trucks entering in the first week of March compared to 4,200 previously. The reduced flow has led to severe shortages, with flour prices tripling and tomatoes more than doubling. Many families have depleted their income sources, further challenging food access. The shortages of food and cooking equipment have suspended the operations of some community kitchens, risking the reversal of food security improvements. ([UNRWA 05/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/unrwa-situation-report-211-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-occupied-west-bank-including-east-jerusalem-enar), [AJ 10/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/10/gaza-food-prices-soar-as-border-closures-deepen-shortages-amid-iran-war), [TNA 19/03/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/gaza-aid-plunges-during-iran-war-israel-tightens-blockade)))

UPDATE 02/03/2026
The risk has deteriorated, with Israel announcing the indefinite closure of crossings into Gaza, including the Rafah border crossing, on 1 March 2026 following the start of the Israel/US war on Iran on 28 February. This has immediately suspended aid flow into the strip and suspended humanitarian operations inside Gaza, including the World Central Kitchen. This will disrupt access to food and spike food prices. The food insecurity deterioration has become highly likely. ([WCK 01/03/2026](https://wck.org/news/media-alert-border-closure-forces-world-central-kitchen-to-pause-gaza-meal-operations/))

UPDATE 24/02/2026
The risk continues to be stable, although the ceasefire between Hamas and Israel agreed on 10 October 2025 remains highly fragile. Between 10 October 2025 and 10 January 2026, at least 1,244 Israeli violations of the ceasefire were recorded, including incursions beyond the yellow line and control of roughly 58–60% of Gaza, particularly in Gaza city, Khan Younis, and Rafah. Humanitarian access is still heavily restricted; aid convoys, medical supplies, and winter relief have been delayed or blocked, worsening conditions for civilians, especially after flooding from Storm Byron in December 2025 affected 55,000 families. ([TNA 15/01/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/gaza-records-over-1200-israeli-ceasefire-violations), [OCHA 18/12/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-349-gaza-strip), [AJ 22/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/politics/2026/2/22/%D9%85%D8%A7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B0%D9%8A-%D8%AA%D8%BA%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D9%88%D8%B5%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AA))

R1065.title: A prolonged Syria–Lebanon border conflict results in displacement and increases shelter and livelihood needs

evolution.rationale_update:
UPDATE 25/04/2026
The risk improved slightly in April 2026 after tensions rose in March with an escalation between Hezbollah and Israel. Because of insecurity at the border, the Syrian transitional Government increased its military presence at Al Masnaa crossing and deployed more forces, establishing at least three new checkpoints and intensifying searches of travellers and vehicles. Tensions in March increased because of artillery shells being fired from Lebanon and landing in western Damascus. On 4 April, the Israeli military announced its intention to strike Al Masnaa crossing, citing Hezbollah's use of it for military purposes and the smuggling of combat equipment and urging residents to evacuate. Lebanese security sources confirmed evacuating the crossing following the Israeli threat. ([TNA 09/03/2026](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/why-tensions-are-rising-syria-lebanon-border), [Al-Monitor 04/04/2026](https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/04/israel-says-will-strike-lebanon-syria-border-crossing))

UPDATE 11/02/2026
Border tensions between Syria and Lebanon have stabilized since late 2025, despite one minor clash near Hermel in December, with both governments pursuing cooperative measures amid underlying security concerns. On 5 February, Lebanon and Syria reached a deal to repatriate approximately 300 Syrian inmates from Lebanese prisons, a priority for Damascus since Al Assad's fall and a signal of improving bilateral relations. However, Damascus filed a separate extradition request for over 200 former regime officers allegedly in Lebanon accused of using Lebanese territory to finance Alawite insurgency operations, led by Brigadier General Suheil Al Hassan and billionaire Rami Makhlouf in Moscow. Syrian authorities continue intercepting weapons and drug smuggling attempts, seizing assault rifles, RPG launchers, Iranian Shahed drones, and ammunition in January heading to Hezbollah via border crossings near Tartous and Sarghaya, alongside ongoing Captagon interdiction efforts. Israeli airstrikes on four Syria–Lebanon border crossings used by Hezbollah for arms smuggling in January complicated dynamics. Turkey has facilitated limited communication between Damascus and Hezbollah to defuse tensions, though Hezbollah justifies retaining weapons citing potential Syrian threats.
([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [Al Jazeera 11/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/2/11/why-is-the-issue-of-syrian-prisoner-repatriation-from-lebanon-complicated), [Le Monde 01/02/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/02/01/between-lebanon-and-syria-the-search-for-a-fresh-start-since-assad-s-fall-and-hezbollah-s-collapse_6750025_4.html), [L'Orient Today 14/12/2025](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1488404/clashes-between-lebanese-army-and-syrian-general-security-agents-near-hermel.html), [Times of Israel 17/01/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/syria-says-it-foiled-attempt-to-smuggle-rifles-drones-into-lebanon-via-illegal-border-crossing/), [Times of Israel 26/01/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/syrias-new-regime-says-it-stopped-weapons-shipment-heading-to-hezbollah-in-lebanon/))


UPDATE 25/11/2025
Tensions on the Syria–Lebanon borders continue to be reported, contributing to the increased likelihood of clashes. On 15 November, residents of Jrajir town in Qalamoun region (of Syria) protested at the informal Zamrani border crossing after the Lebanese army began establishing military points on their privately owned agricultural lands, which contain over 100,000 fruit trees (mainly cherries and apples). These lands have been inaccessible to farmers since 2017, when Syrian government forces and Hezbollah took control of the Qalamoun Mountains. On 13 November, foreign fighters from the Syrian army were redeployed from the Harem area in Idleb governorate to Al Qusayr, near the Syria–Lebanon border, alongside the movement of heavy military equipment and armoured units. At the same time, forces linked to the Ministry of Defense of the Syrian Transitional Government attempted to advance into Lebanese territory in Wadi Al Thalajat in Ras Al Ma‘ara, an area without Lebanese army presence. These deployments took place at the same time as clashes between Syrian army units and cells of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria positioned opposite the Lebanese town of Arsal. ([The Cradle 13/11/2025](https://thecradle.co/articles/exclusive-syria-deploys-foreign-fighters-to-lebanon-border#google_vignette), [SOHR 15/11/2025](https://www.syriahr.com/%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC-%D8%B4%D8%B9%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AC%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%AC%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%81-%D8%AF%D9%85%D8%B4%D9%82-%D8%B6%D8%AF-%D8%A5%D9%86%D8%B4%D8%A7/784475/))

UPDATE 05/09/2025
In September, media reports indicated that Hezbollah was working to retrieve weapons stored in Syria, including former Syrian army stockpiles and arms held by Iranian-backed militias, to rebuild capabilities weakened by Israeli strikes. Between July–September, the Syrian Government foiled around 13 smuggling attempts from Syria into Lebanon, most involving weapon shipments. Although Syrian authorities say they control over 75% of the Syria–Lebanon border, security gaps remain, mainly along the rugged border areas near Homs governorate, the Syrian Coast, and Qalamoun region, allowing smuggling operations to continue. ([Majjala 04/09/2025](https://www.majalla.com/node/327209/%D8%B3%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%A9/%D8%AD%D8%B2%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D9%87-%D9%8A%D8%B5%D8%B1-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%A3%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%AD%D8%AA%D9%87-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B2%D9%86%D8%A9-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7))


UPDATE 23/07/2025
The transitional Government continues with efforts to combat the smuggling of drugs and weapons. In July 2025, the Syrian Ministry of Interior confirmed being engaged in a non-publicised security cooperation with Saudi Arabia focused on combating the trafficking of drugs – especially Captagon – and remnants of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. The collaboration includes intelligence sharing, joint operations, and planned Saudi-led training for Syrian personnel. Both sides have held multiple meetings to deepen cooperation across areas including border control, tackling organised crime, and institutional development, with Saudi officials expressing commitment to supporting Syria’s security and stability.
